activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
Brooke had claimed the carrel by the periodicals at three o'clock, and by five she had filled the whole table with folders, a laptop, and a stapler she'd taken from the supply shelf without asking. The application deadline was midnight. She opened the laptop, typed her legal name, and then sat looking at the question about her activities as though the screen might volunteer something first.

"You're going to burn out that outlet," a voice said. A boy from her civics class, Dev, stood at the end of the shelf holding a copy of an engineering magazine he clearly had no intention of reading. "They shut the Wi-Fi at nine now. Council cut the hours."

"I know when they shut the Wi-Fi."

He sat down across from her anyway, uninvited, and turned one of her folders to face himself. "You're doing all fourteen of these tonight?"

"Thirteen." She took the folder back. "Fourteen if the essay survives." She had written about her grandmother's garden, then about quitting piano, and both drafts had ended up saying nothing, careful paragraphs of nothing that any admissions reader would skim past. "It's the same essay going everywhere. Same form, everything. The Common App."

He squinted at her. "You think the college in Vermont wants what the one in Arizona wants?"

The question had been circling her all week, and she had kept swatting it away. "It's one application. It goes to all of them."

"Convenient," Dev said, and she heard the edge under the word, the accusation she'd been making to herself.

At the reference desk, because she refused to argue from memory, she asked the librarian on duty if there was anything on how college applications worked, history-wise, and was pointed to a shelf where an education handbook sat with a cracked spine. She read standing up. In 1975, the book said, the Common Application had been founded with 15 member colleges. She turned pages. More than 1,000 members now. Fifteen schools and a mimeographed form, and now the thing she was feeding her whole self into, one essay to stand for every version of her.

She carried the book back to the carrel. "Guess how many colleges it started with. Fifteen. It's over a thousand now."

"So they made it efficient."

"So they made it cheap to apply everywhere. Which means everyone applies everywhere, which means nobody's application means anything." She heard her own voice climb and lowered it. The woman two tables over looked up from her newspapers. Brooke pressed her palms flat on the table. "That's the argument, anyway. My dad makes it. Apply to fewer schools, mean it somewhere. My mom says the opposite, that it's a system and you use the system you're given, and being circumspect about it is how other people get your spot."

"And you?"

She had spent months refusing to introspect on the question because introspection felt like stalling, like one more draft of the garden essay. But the book was open in front of her, and the number, that original fifteen, had settled something loose in her. "I think they're both describing a real thing. The form makes you generic and it makes you possible. Both at once. I don't think it cancels out."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the answer I have." She closed the book. "My dad keeps saying find the one school, like it's a person. Like there's exactly one. He said it at dinner again last night, and I nodded, because it's a platitude, and platitudes are what he has instead of money." She hadn't meant to say the last part. Dev didn't say anything back, which she appreciated more than sympathy would have been worth.

She opened the laptop. The essay was still the piano one, four paragraphs about quitting and one paragraph pretending she'd learned something. She read it once, honestly, the way she'd been avoiding. Then she cut the last paragraph and wrote three sentences about the night she'd taken the garden essay and the piano essay and realized they were the same essay, both written for nobody in particular, and that she wanted, before any school answered her, to write one thing for somebody in particular even if that somebody was only her.

At nine the Wi-Fi died exactly as Dev had promised. She tethered to her phone, paid for the essay's last look with a warning about her data, and pressed submit at 9:41, thirteen applications gone into the dark, one held back. The one she'd kept was the small school her father had never heard of, the one she had visited alone on a bus in October and liked without being able to say why.

Dev leaned over to watch the confirmation screen load. "Now what?"

"Now we wait until March." She began stacking the folders, and her hands were not quite steady, and she kept stacking anyway.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is exothermic, so low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but industrial plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold.
story:
The chemistry lab smelled of hot dust and somebody's abandoned instant noodles, and Katherine had claimed the corner bench because it was the only one where the radiator actually worked. She spread her revision notes across it like a general planning a campaign she expected to lose.

"You look morose," said Dev, dropping his bag on the stool opposite. He was only in the room because his frees coincided with hers, and because Mrs. Okafor had stopped chasing non-chemistry students out of the lab sometime around October.

"I look like someone doing equilibrium problems." She turned her notebook so he could see. Nitrogen plus hydrogen going to ammonia, arrows pointing both ways, a little rectangle of graph paper where her working had collapsed into cross-hatching. "The principle says if you change the conditions, the system shifts to oppose the change. So if I heat it, it shifts to take the heat back. It goes the wrong way. I can predict that part. I just can't make myself believe anyone cares."

Dev leaned over and read the page upside down, a skill he had refined across years of copying homework he had no intention of understanding. "Why would a factory choose a temperature that gives less product? That seems like the sort of thing a factory wouldn't do."

"That's exactly the question." Katherine sat back. "If making ammonia gives out heat, then low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium. Hot it, and the balance slides backward, away from what you want. The Haber process should be run in a freezer. Every textbook problem says so, and every textbook problem is three lines long."

"So what's the problem?"

She looked at him, and then at the radiator, which had begun its afternoon complaint, a ticking like a small animal trapped in the pipes. The heat was the point, she thought. Not the conclusion, but the choosing. "The problem is that the problems are lying by omission. There's a whole part of the world the exam doesn't want me to look at."

She went to the shelf where Mrs. Okafor kept the old reference books, the ones nobody signed out, and pulled down the industrial chemistry volume with the cracked spine. She read standing up, one hip against the bench, while Dev ate crisps with the refinement of a man feeding a furnace. What she found made her sit down slowly, the way you sit when a thing you already half-knew gets confirmed.

"They run it hot," she said. "Industrial plants. Hotter than the temperature that would give the most ammonia. On purpose."

"That's stupid."

"It's not stupid, it's the opposite of stupid. It's just not equilibrium." She tapped the page without showing it to him, guarding it like a card. "At low temperature you get the most ammonia sitting there in the balance, but the reaction is too slow when cold. Too slow to be anything. The yield is beautiful and nothing happens. You'd own a perfect amount of a substance you'd wait a geological age to collect."

Dev considered this with his mouth full. "So the factory wants speed, and the exam wants the maximum."

"And I have to hold both of them in my head at the same time and write down only one." She laughed, briefly, without much humour in it. "It problematizes the whole principle, honestly. Not the chemistry, the chemistry is fine. The teaching of it. It gives you a rule for the perfect balance and then grades you as if the perfect balance were the whole of engineering."

She began copying the diagram into her notes, the double arrow drawn with real care this time, and under it she wrote the temperature figures in her smallest hand. She was aware of a small private shift, the kind that no mark scheme would ever record: she had spent two years thinking of chemistry as a set of answers, and now she could see that some of its answers were answers to questions nobody actually asked. The equilibrium yield was true. The industrial temperature was also true. What stayed uncertain was which truth you were obliged to serve, and she suspected the honest answer was that you served whichever one was standing in front of you at the time.

Mrs. Okafor came through to collect the glassware, saw the open reference book, and raised an eyebrow at Katherine's notes.

"You do realise," she said, "that none of that is on the syllabus. On Thursday they will ask you one thing: which way does the equilibrium shift when you heat it."

"Backward," Katherine said. "Away from ammonia."

"Good. Write that."

Katherine wrote it. Then, underneath, in ordinary handwriting, not hidden but not advertised, she added: but they run it hot anyway.

Dev read it upside down and frowned. "Is that going to cost you marks?"

"Probably," she said, and put the pen down. "Do you want the rest of these crisps or not?"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
The festival took over four blocks of Maple Street, and by six o'clock the whole neighborhood smelled of charcoal and charoset. Alexa's family claimed a stretch of curb near the stage where the rabbi's table had been set up for the public Seder, white cloth pinned against the wind. Her grandmother unwrapped the old Haggadah from a dish towel and smoothed it flat, the way she did every year, and Alexa noticed that the book had gone to the long table this time instead of to their own blanket. Her mother had volunteered it without asking. That was the first thing wrong with the evening.

The second thing was her cousin Dov, who was twelve and had the Four Questions. He had earned them the hard way: he was the youngest child present from any of the three families sharing the table, and the rabbi's own granddaughter, who was nine, had backed out that afternoon with a fever. Dov had been talking about the questions for a week, and now he stood behind the folding chairs with the photocopied page in his fist, saying nothing, going gray.

"You're on in twenty minutes," Alexa told him.

"I can't."

"You've known this since you were six."

"That was at Grandma's house." He crumpled the page partway and then smoothed it against his knee, as if the paper were the problem. "There's two hundred people out here."

She could have let it go. She wanted, honestly, to be at the front table herself, holding the Haggadah her grandmother's mother had carried out of Salonika, but the custom was the custom: the youngest child present asked the questions, beginning with the one everyone knew, "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Alexa had asked them herself at seven, in a voice so small her uncle had leaned in to hear, and she remembered the weight of it, all those adults waiting. There was something in that memory she still couldn't decide about, whether the tradition honored the youngest or simply used them, whether making a child carry the opening of the Seder problematized the whole idea of welcoming the stranger, or was exactly what welcoming meant.

"Okay," she said. "Stand up. Now."

He stood. A man selling fried dough shouted past them, choleric at his register, and Dov flinched, and Alexa put herself between the shout and her cousin.

"First line."

"Why is this night different..." He stopped. "Different from all other nights."

"Again. Louder than feels right. Out here everything eats your voice."

They ran it six times. She made him sing it to the traffic on Maple, to a woman waiting for the port-a-john, to a group of college kids who slowed down and listened, which was worse for Dov than any silence, and he knew it, and he got through it anyway. By the seventh run he was doing the sequence without the paper: the dipping twice, the reclining, the bitter herbs, the bread of affliction. His voice found a rhythm that belonged to him rather than to his fear.

Then her grandmother appeared at the front table, holding the old Haggadah up like a signal flag. "The rabbi wants the book for the reading," she called. "And the boy, when it's time. Where is the boy?"

Dov looked at Alexa. The lights on the stage came up, and the rabbi was already saying something about the order of the evening, about who asks and why, and two hundred people settled into their chairs.

"You're the youngest one here," Alexa said. "That's you. Go."

"The book," he said. "I can't read Grandma's. It's Ladino on one side."

"So don't read it. You know it. Sing it at the sky."

He walked up the middle of the aisle with the photocopy and then, at the table, folded it away in his pocket and took the old Haggadah from their grandmother, who held on one second longer than she needed to before letting go. The rabbi gestured for quiet. Dov put his hand flat on the page, and Alexa stood on her toes at the back of the crowd, and her mother's hand landed on her shoulder without a word.

"Why is this night different from all other nights?" Dov asked, and the whole street went quiet enough to hear the fryer hissing two blocks away, and then he went on to the second question, and then the third, and Alexa stopped counting and just listened.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A margin of error is expressed in percentage points, not percent: plus or minus 3 points on a 58 percent result means a likely range of 55 to 61 percent.
story:
The campaign office smelled of burnt coffee and wet cardboard, and Avery had been there for forty minutes before anyone asked who she was. She had written "student journalist" on her nametag in handwriting that suddenly looked young to her, so she pressed her thumb over the word whenever anyone glanced at her. Along one wall, volunteers worked phones in a low murmur, and above the copier someone had taped the new poll results on a sheet of butcher paper, the numbers fat and black: 58 percent.

Avery had come for the school paper. Her editor, Devon, had wanted the piece by Friday, and he had wanted it loud. "Lead cut in half, that's the story," he had texted her, and in her draft that was the lede, followed by the poll and a line about the margin of error, which she had written from memory: plus or minus 3 percent of 58 percent. It had sounded right when she typed it. It sounded right again when she read it on the bus. Now, standing in front of the butcher paper with her notebook open, she couldn't remember where she had learned it, and the not remembering sat in her stomach like a stone.

She copied the poll numbers down, then drifted toward the front desk, where a woman named Priya was stapling walk lists. Avery asked about the poll, and Priya pointed her toward a stack of printed memos bound with a rubber band. "Everything we're allowed to say is in there," Priya said, and went back to the stapler.

Avery carried the memo to a folding table by the window and read it in the gray light. The language was duller than she expected, all caveats and footnotes, but one line stopped her: the margin of error was expressed in percentage points. Plus or minus 3 points on a result of 58 percent meant a likely range of 55 to 61 percent. She read the line twice, then set the draft of her article beside it on the table.

She took out a pencil. In her draft, the margin of error was "3 percent of 58 percent," which would have been a sliver, barely more than one and a half. She looked from her notebook to the memo and back, and felt a slow, cold sense of foreboding spread through her, the kind that comes not from danger but from realizing how confidently you can be wrong. Her version had made the poll look nearly exact. The truth made it a wide band. Under her pencil, she drew the actual range, 55 to 61, and saw that everything Devon wanted to claim about momentum could dissolve inside it.

Devon answered on the second ring. "Tell me you have the numbers."

"I have them. But the margin of error part in my draft is wrong. It's points, not percent," she said. "Three points. So 58 could really be anywhere from 55 to 61."

There was a pause long enough that she could hear a television in his background. Then he said, "That's the same thing," in a tone she recognized, the petulant drawl he used when a fact got between him and a headline.

"It's not the same thing," she said. "One of them makes the race look decided. The other one makes it look like anything." She kept her voice level, the way the phone bank volunteers did, and watched rain start to dot the window beside her.

He argued for a while, then went quiet, then asked what she wanted to do. She told him she wanted to run the range, 55 to 61, plainly, and let the readers see how much room was in it, even if it made a softer story. She admitted she didn't know whether the lead had really been cut or not; the numbers didn't say, and she wasn't willing to pretend they did. Devon said he'd look at it, which was not yes, and hung up.

Avery gathered her things slowly. On her way out, Priya was taping a fresh sheet to the wall, a reminder about Saturday canvassing, and Avery stopped to read it though she didn't have to. Behind her, the phones kept up their murmuring, and someone laughed near the coffee machine. She put her notebook in her bag, zipped it, and pushed open the door into the rain.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
story:
Edouard had been at the kitchen table for two hours, laptop open, the personal statement drafted and redrafted until the words had gone smooth and meaningless, like a stone handled too long. Amelie had sent him her old statement in the spring, back when he first mentioned applying, with a note that said: this got me five offers, steal whatever you want. He had stolen the structure, the opening anecdote about taking apart a radio, the closing paragraph that tied ambition to gratitude. Tonight he meant to paste it into the form and be finished.

His sister Colette sat across from him with her homework, which she was doing in a way that involved a great deal of drawing on her wrist. "You're still on that?" she said.

"Checking the character count." He scrolled through the portal to the section marked personal statement, ready to paste, and then stopped. There was no box. There were three of them, each with its own question above it, and a counter beneath each that read zero.

"Problem?" Colette said, without looking up.

"There's supposed to be one statement." He read the first question. Why do you want to study this subject? Then the second, about how he had prepared, and a third he had to read twice. "This isn't the form Amelie described."

"So message her."

She was in Lisbon, two hours ahead, but she answered on the second ring, her face pixelating against a hostel wall. "Edouard. It's late there."

"The form's changed. It's three questions now, not one statement. Did you know that?"

"No. When did they do that?" She looked genuinely thrown, and he found that almost worse than the problem itself, because Amelie was the person in the family who knew things. "Mine was just one long box. Four thousand characters, say something clever in the first line, that was the whole game."

"That's what I wrote." He turned the laptop so she could see the three empty boxes, the questions sitting above them like invigilators. "It says the change started with people applying for 2026 entry. That's me."

"Then your opening anecdote is dead," she said. "The radio thing was for a single narrative. Three questions want three answers." She paused, someone behind her laughing at something. "Look, the advice that mattered wasn't the structure anyway. It was: don't denigrate other subjects to make yours look better. Admissions people hate that."

"I never do that."

"You wrote 'unlike the vagueness of English.' I read your draft."

He closed the call not long after, telling her to enjoy Lisbon, and she said something about how the city was not nearly as hedonistic as their father claimed, and then he sat looking at the first question. Why did he want to study engineering? The honest answer had a shape he didn't like. Part of it was the radio, taken apart at eleven, the copper coil like a small brass nest. Part of it was that engineering was respectable, that their father approved of it, that it led somewhere with a salary. Part of it was simply that he was good at physics and had let the good narrow the choice the way a river narrows into a channel without deciding anything.

Colette had stopped drawing on herself and was watching him. "You look like you're arguing with someone."

"I'm deciding whether to lie."

"That seems easy."

"It's not lying lying. It's choosing which true thing to say." He thought of the boys at his school who talked about their fathers' firms, the placements arranged over dinners he would never attend, a small oligarchy of connections that no personal statement could compete with and that he was not supposed to resent. He could write around all that, or he could write the version where he admitted the radio was partly an escape from a bedroom he shared with Colette, where the preparation was a job at the garden centre and a library card and YouTube, and nothing that cost money.

He began typing into the first box. He wrote about the radio, then deleted the graceful part and left the clumsy part, which was that he had broken it permanently and learned more from that than from fixing anything. In the second box, about preparation, he listed the garden centre, the broken lawnmower engines, the maths he did for fun on the bus. The third question he answered in nine sentences, and none of them were clever.

When he finished, near midnight, Colette had gone to bed and the counters showed numbers well under the limits, so much space unused that it felt like leaving a room half-furnished. He read it once through and could not tell whether it was better than Amelie's version or only barer. He moved the cursor to submit, then stopped, and read the first line again.

"Why do I want this," he said to the empty kitchen, and typed one more sentence at the top of the first box.

"There," he said, and pressed the button.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
Paige had never once been wrong about anything at a Super Bowl party, which was a thing she could say because nobody kept records. The rink's banquet room smelled of nacho cheese and skate oil, the TV bolted high above the rental counter, and the whole extended family had been herded in between periods of public skating because Aunt Renata refused to miss the game and Cousin Dex refused to miss the ice. Paige sat between the two loyalties with her chemistry textbook open on her knees, half watching the screen, half watching everything else, because that was what she was good at, noticing.

Grandpa Walt planted himself in front of the television with a paper cup of coffee he would never admit was decaf. "You kids don't know what a Super Bowl is," he announced, which was how he began most sentences. "I remember the first one. I was there, matter of fact. Saw it with my own two eyes. Best day of my life, outside of marrying your grandmother."

Dex snorted without looking up from lacing his skates. "You were there, Grandpa?"

"In person. Front row, practically."

Paige did not verbalize her doubt, because she had learned that arguing with Grandpa Walt was like arguing with the Zamboni, but something snagged in her mind the way a skater's blade catches a rut. She pulled out her phone under the table, angling it away from Aunt Renata, who confiscated phones on principle.

The chemistry chapter, meanwhile, was staring up at her from her lap, all about polymers, and she let her eyes drift down to it while the search loaded. A polymer was just a chain, and a monomer was a single link, one small unit that seemed like nothing on its own until it repeated and connected and became something you couldn't snap with your hands. Families, she thought, were like that. One dinner, one argument, one Super Bowl party, none of it mattered much alone.

The page came up. The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles. She read it twice, then a third time, because a fact like that deserved a slow look. Grandpa Walt had been born, as far as she knew, in a small town in Ohio, and he had told the story of his one trip to California a hundred times, and in that story he was nineteen and it involved a girl named Carol and a broken-down Pontiac, and it had happened, by Paige's arithmetic, several years after 1967. Which meant he had been nowhere near Los Angeles that day. Or the Ohio math was wrong. Or the hundred tellings of the Pontiac story had drifted, the way stories drift, the way she herself might already be misremembering the Pontiac story right now, sitting here believing her own memory was a camera when really it was more like Grandpa's.

She looked up at him. He had gone quiet, watching the screen with his cup cradled in both hands, and there was something in his face she did not usually let herself see, because noticing was easier when you kept it shallow. He looked like a man at a window. He had a congenital heart thing, the family murmured, an arrhythmia he'd had since birth, and every year the game got a little louder around it.

Paige thought about the fact in her hand, small and hard and exact, one little monomer of the truth. She could march over and set it down in front of him. The first Super Bowl, she would say, was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles, and you were not there. It would be accurate. It would also be like throwing a puck at the window just to prove glass could break. Maybe he knew it was false and told it anyway, the way you keep a photograph of a place you've only imagined. Maybe he half knew. Maybe she was wrong about Ohio, wrong about the Pontiac, wrong about all of it, and the only thing she could be sure of was the sentence on her screen, and even certainty, she was starting to suspect, was just doubt that hadn't been tested yet.

Dex clattered onto the ice through the far door and fell almost immediately, waving cheerfully through the glass. Grandpa laughed, a real laugh, and pointed with his cup.

On the television a receiver caught the ball at the sideline and both teams reset, and Paige closed the phone and slid it into her pocket, the fact still sitting in her like something swallowed whole. She would keep it. She wasn't sure yet whether she'd ever use it, and that, at least, felt honest.

She stood, tucked the chemistry book under her arm, and walked toward the rink door to watch Dex fall again.

"There she goes," Grandpa called after her. "Write that down, Paigey. Your granddad saw the first one."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
Landon had claimed the cooking duty at the campsite with the confidence of a boy who had watched exactly four cooking videos and internalized none of them. The family soup, his mother had decreed, was his contribution to the trip, and so he stood at the picnic table with a cutting board, a dull knife, and an onion the size of a softball, while his younger sister Marisa read a paperback in the folding chair beside him.

The first cut went badly in a way he had not anticipated. He halved the onion, began dicing, and within thirty seconds Marisa slammed her book shut, wiped her eyes with her sleeve, and announced, voice wobbling, "Something's attacking me."

"You're crying over an onion," Landon said. "That's genuinely pathetic."

"I'm not crying. My eyes are on fire."

"It's fine to cry," he said, magnanimous, dicing on. "I won't tell anyone at school that my sister weeps over produce."

She threw a pinecone at him. He ducked, laughing, and then the vapor reached his own eyes and the laughing stopped quite abruptly. He turned away from the table, blinking hard, and Marisa said, with terrible relish, "Oh, now who's crying over produce," and Landon, eyes streaming, said, "Neither of us is crying, that's the whole point," and then had to stop talking because his throat had closed around the word "point."

He walked to the cooler, splashed water on his face, and thought back to the summer before, when his grandfather had sat on the porch shelling peas and told him about his own father, a chemist who had kept a jar of something or other on the kitchen windowsill. Landon had been twelve and mostly interested in the popsicles, but he remembered one detail now with sudden clarity: the old man saying that onions were chemistry, that the tears were not sentiment but a reaction, and that anyone who mocked a person for crying at an onion was mocking science itself. Landon had not understood, and his grandfather's explanation had been long, prolix even, full of words that slid off a twelve-year-old like rain off a poncho.

Now, blinking at the cutting board, he took out his phone, held it at arm's length with one eye shut, and searched. It took him a minute of squinting through water to find it, and when he did, he read it aloud, half to Marisa and half to the sky. "Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear."

"Say that again," Marisa said.

"Syn-propanethial-S-oxide," Landon said, carefully, tasting the syllables like a foreign candy. "It's a vapor. It floats up off the cut cells and attacks your eyes. It's not emotion. It's not weakness. It is a chemical ambush."

"So we're both victims of chemistry," Marisa said.

"We are casualties of science," Landon said. "I take back everything I said." He considered this for a moment, holding the knife still against the board. There was something in it that interested him beyond the excuse for his stinging eyes: the way the same fact could make teasing seem both crueler and sillier at once. His instinct had been to mock; the truth said the mockery had no target, that Marisa's tears were as involuntary as a sneeze. But it also meant his apology was easy, purchased with a fact rather than with anything harder. He wasn't sure those two things balanced. He filed the question away, the way his mother filed receipts, somewhere retrievable.

He tried the folk remedies. He put on his sunglasses, which helped approximately nothing and made Marisa laugh so hard she had to leave the table. He chewed bread, which his mother swore by and which accomplished nothing except making him look like a hamster in distress. Finally he cut the rest of the onion underwater in the wash bin, and when no vapor reached anyone's eyes, he felt enfranchised by his own learning, a citizen of the republic of not weeping.

"This is my heuristic now," he told Marisa, pointing the knife at the bin. "Onion plus water equals dignity."

"You learned that an hour ago."

"All wisdom is recent if you live long enough," Landon said, which he thought was possibly profound, and poured the diced onion into the pot, where it hissed against the oil and filled the campsite with a smell so good that even Marisa, still sniffling, drifted back toward the fire.

Their mother came up from the lake, took one look at the table, the wash bin, the sunglasses lying in the dirt, and said, "Why is everyone's face swollen?"

"Chemistry, Mom," Marisa said. "Ask Landon. He's a citizen now."

Landon opened his mouth to explain, and the wind, obliging to the last, shifted direction off the cutting board where the onion skins still sat, and both of his eyes filled instantly with tears.

"Not crying," he said, wiping his face with the hem of his shirt. "Chemistry."
