fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
story:
The stadium smelled like spilled beer and cold air, and Rosalie's grandfather had already claimed his seat in the second row of the club level, directly behind the glass, before anyone else in the family had found the right stairwell. It was Game Seven, and his team was down by one going into the third period. He had waited, he told anyone who would listen, forty-one years for a night like this.

The trouble started before the puck dropped. Her uncle Rick, who had come only because his sister, Rosalie's mother, had insisted, kept checking his phone and saying things like "wake me when it's over." He denigrated the whole sport at dinner beforehand, calling it men with sticks and no dental plan, and now he was doing it again in a low mutter that Grandpa could obviously hear. Rosalie's cousin Theo, who was facetious about almost everything, offered to sell Rick his seat for twenty dollars, which didn't help, though it made her mother laugh into her scarf.

On the jumbotron between whistles, a trivia question appeared: which trophy, first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America? Rosalie knew it before she finished reading. She had known it since she was eleven, since the summer after her grandmother died, when Grandpa sat her down at the kitchen table with the old encyclopedia and told her the whole thing himself. The Cup had been donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston, he had said, tapping the page with two fingers, and first awarded in 1893, and nothing older still existed for any professional team on the continent. It was older than every player on the ice tonight, older than the arena, older than Rick.

"Stanley Cup," she said out loud, quietly, and Theo gave her a look of mock astonishment, and the screen confirmed it a moment later with a burst of confetti graphics.

What she hadn't known, until this evening, was that her grandfather had almost sold the tickets. Her mother confessed it in the concourse while they waited in line for hot chocolate. He'd had an offer, a good one, from a broker at his church, and he'd sat on it for a week, because the property tax bill had come and his pension, as he put it, was a rumor that kept not arriving. He had decided to keep them only that morning. Rosalie thought of last October, when he'd invited her to his birthday dinner and she'd stayed home instead to study for a calculus exam, telling herself the session mattered, that there would be other birthdays. She had gotten the grade she wanted. It had cost her nothing, apparently, except that now she counted things like that.

She carried the hot chocolate back down the stairs carefully, and it was somewhere around the eighth minute of the third that the game tied itself up, and then, with four minutes left, untied itself in the other direction. Grandpa was on his feet with his hands in the air, and Rick was on his feet too, though he would deny it later. Theo had his phone out, filming his grandfather filming the ice, a video of a video of a man watching the thing he'd waited four decades for.

Between the tying goal and the winning one, Rosalie found herself thinking about a lemma her math teacher kept returning to, some small proven statement that you accepted so that larger arguments could be built on top of it. She had never liked that word as a girl; it sounded like a disclaimer. But tonight the oldest fact she knew, a trophy donated by a governor general in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, was holding up a whole family in a cold building in the third period, and the fact seemed less like trivia than like a foundation, something to stand on while everything else wobbled. Whether that was a real thought or just the scoreboard talking, she couldn't have said.

When the horn sounded, Grandpa didn't cheer. He sat back down, put his hat over his heart, and stayed there while the arena detonated around him, streamers falling from the rafters onto the heads of people who hadn't waited forty-one years for anything. Rosalie sat down beside him and put her hand flat on the back of his neck, the way her grandmother used to. The players were lining up to shake hands, an old custom, and her grandfather watched every single one of them do it.

"He would have hated this," Theo said into the roar, meaning his own father, meaning Rick, who was crying a little and pretending it was the cold. Rosalie didn't answer. She was watching the tunnel, where a silver bowl older than everyone in the building was being wheeled out toward the ice on a padded cart, two men in gloves walking beside it the whole way.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In Westminster-style parliaments such as the UK's, the second reading is a debate and vote on a bill's general principles, before its details are examined.
story:
The bill had started as Alexa's homework, one page of careful clauses about letting sixteen-year-olds vote in municipal elections, and now it sat on the overhead projector while twenty-three classmates pretended to be the House of Commons. Ms. Okafor had divided the class with playing cards pulled from a shoebox: red for government, black for opposition, jokers for the Speaker's table. Alexa had drawn a red seven, which meant she was supposed to defend a bill she had written herself, a strange position, like being asked to argue for her own existence.

"First reading is just the introduction," Ms. Okafor had said on Monday, holding up the shoebox. "No debate. You publish the bill and it's on the record. The real work starts after that." She would not say more. She had a habit of answering questions by pointing at the procedure binder on the front desk, its plastic tabs labelled in fading marker, and telling them the rules lived there, not in her.

The debate began well enough. Priya, voluble as always, rose from the opposition benches to say that the bill was a plot to disenfranchise taxpayers by diluting their votes with teenagers who, in her words, "cannot yet be trusted to operate a slow cooker." The class laughed. Alexa stood to respond, and she was halfway through a point about school boards making decisions for people who could not vote for them when Marcus raised his hand and did not wait to be called.

"Point of order," he said, with the gravity of a man uncovering chicanery. "Clause two, subsection b. There's a comma after the word 'residency' that shouldn't be there. As written, it changes the meaning of the whole qualifications section." He held up his photocopy, which he had annotated in three colors of pen, as if the comma were a fingerprint at a crime scene. "How can we vote on a bill that says something it doesn't intend to say?"

For ten minutes the chamber argued about the comma. Someone moved to amend it. Someone else said the amendment itself needed a comma. Priya declared that if the drafting was sloppy, the thinking must be sloppy too, and Alexa felt the ground shifting under her, the whole debate sliding sideways into punctuation while the actual question, whether sixteen-year-olds deserved a say, sat untouched on the projector like a guest nobody had greeted.

She went to the binder. She hadn't planned to; her hand just reached for it while Marcus recited the comma rule from some style guide on his phone. Under the tab marked READINGS she found a paragraph about Westminster procedure, and she read it twice, and something in her went quiet and then loud. She stood.

"Speaker," she said. "This is the second reading. It's a debate and vote on the bill's general principles. The details get examined after, line by line, in committee. So the comma isn't before us yet." She looked at Marcus, whose pen was still hovering. "It's a bad comma. You're probably right about it. But it's not this debate."

Marcus frowned at his three colors. "So we just ignore that it's wrong?"

"No. We fix it later, where fixing belongs. Right now the question is whether the idea is worth fixing at all."

Priya stood, and for once she didn't speak immediately. "I still think you're handing the franchise to people who can't drive after nine," she said, "but fine. On principle, then." She sat down, and Alexa understood that this was Priya's version of a gift, and that Priya had wanted all along to argue the big argument, not the comma, that the comma had been Marcus's want, his three colors of proof that he was the smartest person in the room, and both of them had been briefly using the same lever.

The vote came. Fourteen hands for, nine against, the bill passing on its general principles, and Alexa wrote on the margin of her copy: second reading, principles; committee, details. It seemed strange to her that a parliament would split the work that way, and also strangely honest, an admission that ideas and their wording live in different rooms and must be visited separately. She wondered whether her own opinions worked the same way, whether she believed things in principle that she would quarrel with in the particulars. She thought of her brother, twenty-two, who hadn't voted in the last election because, he said, one ballot changed nothing, and she thought that in principle she disagreed with him, though she couldn't yet say exactly where her disagreement would break down into clauses.

The bell rang. Marcus stayed behind, sorting his pens. "Bring it to committee on Thursday," he said, not looking up. "I'll have the comma fixed by then. And subsection d is a mess too."

"Subsection d is fine," Alexa said.

"It's a mess," said Marcus, and clicked his pen twice.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries.
story:
The whiteboard appeared on the first Monday of December, propped against the boards by the zamboni gate, and on it Dana the trainer had drawn four stick figures landing on one leg with their knees bent. Underneath she had written a schedule: single-leg hops, lateral holds, cutting drills, ten minutes before every practice, all season. Evan read it twice while lacing his skates. Behind him, Marcus Delgado read it once and said, to no one in particular, that they were a hockey team, not a yoga studio.

Marcus had a reason for his impatience. In February a junior scout from the conference was coming to watch the team's last stretch of games, and Marcus, who had waited two years for a starting spot on defense, counted every minute of ice time like a man counting money he was owed. Ten minutes of hopping in place was ten minutes gone from breakouts and power plays. The resentment did not fade after the first practice; it metastasized, spreading down the bench in low remarks, until even the quiet goalies were rolling their eyes during the balance holds.

Evan was less sure of his own position than he pretended to be. In his rhetoric seminar that term he had learned to name the parts of an argument, and he had noticed that both sides of the locker-room dispute ran mostly on pathos. Marcus had pride and urgency; Dana had authority and a whistle. Nobody had produced what his professor would have called logos, the actual reasoning, the evidence underneath the claim. So on Thursday, while the others shot pucks at empty nets, he drifted over to where Dana was coiling a jump rope near the whiteboard and asked her, plainly, why the routine was shaped the way it was.

She didn't lecture. She said Dana rarely lectured, which was part of why people trusted her, that she had run the same program at a club up north, and that they could talk after if he wanted the details, and then she blew her whistle for the hop series. He did the hops. He noticed, without deciding to, that the kid next to him, a sophomore named Peter, kept wobbling on the single-leg landings, knees collapsing inward every time he came down.

Afterward, in the corridor outside the weight room, Dana gave him the one thing he had asked for, in the flat tone of someone stating a schedule rather than making a case. The program trained balance, landing technique and cutting technique, she said, because warm-ups built on those things had been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. That was all she claimed for it, and the modesty of the claim was what made it land. No promises about performance, nothing about Marcus's scouts. Just that word, risk, and the quiet verb reduce.

Evan carried it back to the bench the next week, but not as ammunition. He found himself in an awkward middle position, which he could feel the team pressuring him to abandon. When Marcus complained again, Evan said only, "It lowers the chance of blowing out a knee," and Marcus said, "So does luck," and the discussion should have ended there, except that it didn't, because Peter went down in the Saturday game.

It was ugly and ordinary at once, the way injuries are. Peter cut hard to avoid a check, his skate caught a rut, and he folded onto the ice holding his leg, and the arena went very quiet, the way large cold rooms do. The trainer knelt with him; the game stopped; boreal light from the high windows lay in long pale bars across the scratched surface. Peter skated off with help, favoring the ankle, not the knee, and it turned out to be a sprain, two weeks, nothing structural. He would be fine. In the locker room afterward, no one said anything about the whiteboard, and the silence had more than one meaning, and Evan did not try to sort them out loud.

He sat tying his skates the next Monday, in the blue half-dark before the lights came fully up, and watched Marcus at the far end of the room. Marcus was the last one dressed, always, because he liked to walk out last, and today, when he stood, he stood a moment with his weight on one foot, testing his balance the way the routine had taught them, an idle private gesture that no one else saw. Evan laced his last eyelet, stood, and found his own wobble on the left leg, the one that had always been worse, still there. He steadied it, and skated out onto the fresh ice.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark chocolate, around 29-30 degrees Celsius, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.
story:
Elizabeth arrived at the community kitchen on Delancey Street twenty minutes early, which was unusual for her, and stood at the door watching Mrs. Okafor's Saturday class arrange stainless steel bowls on the long counter. She had signed up because her college essay was due in eleven days and she had nothing to write about except grades, which she suspected was like submitting a résumé as a love letter. Her mother had said, learn something with your hands. Her father, who read the news aloud at breakfast like a man delivering verdicts, had said the whole country was becoming a plutocracy where even dessert was a luxury good, and that if she wanted to understand value she should learn to make things people wanted. She was not sure either of them was right, but here she was, tying an apron.

The first weeks were custards and bread, forgiving things. Chocolate was different. Mrs. Okafor handed out thermometers and said only that chocolate had opinions, and that they would find out what they were. On the board she had written a single number, 32, and beside it the word dark, and then, lower down and half erased, something Elizabeth could not read. Elizabeth copied the 32 into her notebook and underlined it twice.

She chose dark chocolate for her first attempt because dark seemed like the adult choice. She chopped it, melted it over the water bath, stirred, cooled it against the marble slab, watching the thermometer the way you watch a sleeping animal. When the mercury read 32 she poured the chocolate into the little molds Mrs. Okafor kept in a bin by the sink, bars shaped like leaves. She waited. In twenty minutes the dark bars had set with a gloss so deep it seemed to transfix the fluorescent light, holding it rather than reflecting it, and when she snapped one the sound was clean, like a knuckle cracking once.

The woman beside her, a nursing student named Priya who talked through everything she did, had chosen milk chocolate because her nephews refused anything darker. Priya melted, cooled, tested, and poured at 32, exactly as Elizabeth had, in the same molds, on the same counter, and the two of them stood over her tray like witnesses at a disaster that refused to occur. Nothing happened. The chocolate stayed soft and dull, thickening slowly into something that looked like candle wax left in a car. Priya touched it with one finger and left a print.

"It's not fair," Priya said. "I did everything you did."

Elizabeth wanted to say that fairness had nothing to do with it, that thermometers do not negotiate, but she had learned in the last month that this was the thing she liked about kitchens: complaining changed nothing except the mood. She scraped Priya's failed batch back into the bowl and started her own milk chocolate instead, because it seemed cowardly to hand over advice she had not tested. She melted it, cooled it on the slab, and watched the thermometer fall past 32, past 31. At 30 the chocolate on the spatula still looked greasy. She kept stirring. At 29 it suddenly did something she could only describe as deciding: it smoothed out, lost its grain, gathered itself around the spatula like silk. She poured it into the leaf molds quickly, before she could think of a reason to doubt it.

While the tray sat cooling, she went looking for the erased words on the board and found Mrs. Okafor's recipe binder open on the desk by the window. In the margin of a page headed milk, in pencil, in the same looping hand, was a note: milk chocolate works around 29 to 30 degrees, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter. Elizabeth read it three times. She felt something almost atavistic, the old satisfaction of finding food that had gone right, something older than grades or essays, and she also felt slightly cheated, because the answer had been sitting in a binder the whole time.

The bars set. Priya snapped one above her head like a celebration and ate half of it before speaking. "Same chocolate," she said, mouth full. "Same everything. It was the temperature."

"Milk fat softens the cocoa butter," Elizabeth said. "That's what the note says. So it needs to be cooler."

"Then why does the board only say dark?"

Elizabeth had wondered this herself, standing at the desk. She thought Mrs. Okafor erased things on purpose, the way she said chocolate had opinions instead of reciting numbers, and Elizabeth still could not decide whether that was a kindness or a cruelty. A person could waste a whole batch learning what a sentence would have told her. But she had also felt the milk chocolate change under her spatula at 29, had felt it in her wrist before she read it anywhere, and she did not think a sentence could have given her that. Maybe both things were true. She carried the tray back to the counter, set a finished bar in front of Priya, and lifted the second one toward the light.

"Snap it," Elizabeth said.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together.
story:
The truck smelled like cardboard and her father's coffee, and Maelie had been riding with her knees against the glove compartment since the state line. Behind them, in the stacked boxes marked MAELIE in her mother's handwriting, was most of what she owned, including the shoebox of notes Priya had passed her over four years of shared classes. Her father drove with the saturnine concentration of a man who believed the truck's mirrors were lying to him. Every few miles he said, "Still in the lane," to no one.

"I keep doing the math," Maelie said, somewhere past the second rest stop. "There was this study. Jeffrey Hall, 2018. He figured out that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together. I read it back in junior year for a psych paper and I didn't think about it again until last night."

Her father glanced over. "Two hundred hours. That's nothing. That's, what, a week."

"It's not nothing." She unrolled the window an inch and let the highway roar in. "I did it for Priya and me. First period, freshman year, through June. Lunch, the walks home, the weekends at her house, the summer her grandmother was sick and I basically lived there. It came out to over three thousand hours. Probably more, because I only counted the parts I could remember, and you forget hours, you don't remember them." She stopped, aware she had been talking too long, and put her hand flat on the shoebox between her feet.

Her father was quiet for half a mile. Then he said, "So you're saying you can't just do it again."

"I'm saying it's not a personality thing. It's not like I'm good at friends and this new town will recognize that. It's hours. It's sitting next to someone for a year and a half before anything counts." She had been trying to ruminating on this all morning, turning it over like a stone, and saying it out loud made it both smaller and heavier.

At the third rest stop, while her father inspected a tire with theatrical suspicion, Maelie sat on the truck's warm tailgate and opened Priya's last message, sent at six that morning.

Do NOT open the shoebox until you get there, it said. Rules. Also I calculated something. If we videochat every Sunday for three hours, that's 150 hours a year, so by the time we're 40 we'll have more hours than we do now, which honestly feels like a mutualism, like we're two organisms that keep each other alive. I looked that word up to make sure I was using it right. I was. Anyway. Your dad just passed a sign for a town called Bucyrus and I need you to confirm it's real.

She typed: Bucyrus is real. Saw the water tower. Then she added: I found the Hall study again. 200 hours. I keep thinking it means we're done, you and me. Banked. Like we passed some exam nobody can take away. Then I keep thinking it means nobody new gets to start for a really long time, and both feel true. She stared at that, deleted it, wrote it again, and sent it before she could delete it twice.

Priya's reply came as they pulled back onto the highway, and Maelie read it with her phone tilted so her father couldn't see, though he was fully occupied with a passing semi. Or, Priya wrote, it means the new people are already starting their hours today and you don't even know which ones they are yet. Also my mom says hi and also that your dad should stop for lunch, he gets saturnine when he's hungry, which I looked up, and yes I am on a vocabulary arc this morning, deal with it.

Maelie laughed out loud, which surprised her father so much he drifted half a lane and corrected himself with dignity. "Share with the class," he said.

"Later." She put the phone face down on the shoebox, on the two of them, and watched the fields run backward, or seem to, the way everything behind you does. Somewhere ahead was a town full of people who had already started, without knowing it, spending their hours on her. She slid the box closer with her heel.

"Hey," she said. "Can we stop at the first diner we see? I'm starving."

Her father checked the mirror, frowned at it, and took the exit.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
The rink had put the gold medal game on the big screen above the skate rental counter, and by the second period half the public skate had drifted into the lobby to watch. Henry sat on the boards with his skates still laced, his father beside him, his little cousin Priya cross-legged on a rubber mat with a paper flag she had drawn herself, blue and gold and black stripes she insisted matched their grandfather's village.

When the broadcast cut to a wide shot of the arena, the Olympic rings hung above the ice, and Priya held her flag up to the screen. "Which one is mine?" she asked. "Which ring is ours?"

Henry, who had spent a whole unit on Olympic history for a midterm he was still half proud of, said, "They're not anybody's. They're just the Olympic colors. Six of them. They picked them a long time ago because they looked good together." It came out more certain than he felt, the way things did when Priya asked him questions, but she accepted it and lowered her flag, and Henry's father gave him a look he recognized, the look that said an indictment was being prepared.

"You told her that like it was in a book," his father said during the intermission, while the Zamboni flooded the far sheet and Priya went to buy a hot chocolate. "I remember the rings from when I was her age. I always thought they meant the whole world was in them."

Henry shrugged. "They mean the Olympics."

"That's not what I said." His father was not angry; he almost never was. He just held on, patiently, the way he held on to the old songs and the old recipes, to the idea that if a symbol had lasted a hundred years it must be carrying something. "You can't look at those rings and think nobody thought about us."

Henry could and partly did, but he texted Marcus, who had done the same midterm and scored higher, mostly because Marcus checked things. Do the rings mean anything, he typed. Priya wants to know which one is ours.

They watched the third period start. On the glass behind the away net, a sticker version of the rings caught the arena light, five interlocking circles, blue, black, red, yellow, green, on white, and Henry found himself doing what Priya had done, holding an idea up against them, his grandfather's blue and gold stripes, and failing to make it fit cleanly. Gold and yellow argued in his head. His father leaned forward when the tying goal was scored and did not say anything, which for him was loud.

Marcus's message arrived between whistles. "Looked it up because you made me curious. Pierre de Coubertin designed the five rings in 1913. He chose the colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background. So technically the white counts. You owe me a milkshake." Henry read it twice. The last clause sat strangely with him, the fact that the emptiness around the rings was doing the same work as the colors, that something he would have called blank was included on purpose.

He showed his father the phone. His father read it, then read it again, and something in his face loosened. "So somebody did think about us," he said. "Whoever we were, back then."

"Every flag that existed then," Henry said. "That's the whole point. Not one ring per country. All of them in the colors together." He was aware he was half reciting, half arriving somewhere, and that the two felt different. His father's version and Marcus's version were not the same thing, one wanted the rings to hold a particular people, the other wanted them to hold everyone at once, and Henry could not make them stop rubbing against each other, though he noticed he did not want to give either one up.

"Priya," he called, and she came back with her hot chocolate, and he told her about Coubertin and 1913, plainly, without the fake certainty. "So your stripes have blue in them, and the rings have blue. And the white, the part that looks like nothing, that's yours too."

Priya studied the screen, then her flag, then him. "So which ring is mine?"

"None of them," Henry said. "All of them. I'm still working on that part."

She seemed to accept it, the way she accepted most of what he said, and turned back to the game, and Henry, watching the puck move through the neutral zone, thought about how he would have to decide eventually what he believed the symbols carried, or whether believing in them at all was something you could do honestly. Then his father stood up, shouting at a rebound, and Henry stood up with him, still holding his phone, and Priya lifted her paper flag over her head as the goal light went on.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, used a computer model called World3 to link population, food, industry, pollution and resources.
story:
Katherine found the book on the bottom shelf of the public library, wedged between a broken atlas and something about composting. The spine said The Limits to Growth, and inside the cover a stamp gave the year, 1972. She had gone in for the town records, because Mr. Reyes's assignment was due Friday and her group had done nothing. Build a model, he had said. Show how the town's growth affects its water supply. Her group had produced one poster with a sad-looking lake drawn in marker.

"Can I check this out?" she asked at the desk. The librarian turned it over twice, as if it might be dead.

The book had been done for something called the Club of Rome, Katherine read on the bus, by a team at MIT. They had built a computer model, and the model linked five things: population, food, industry, pollution, resources. She read the sentence three times. The model had a name, World3, and the name appeared on every page like a character in a novel.

At school the next morning, Devon was waiting by her locker with his phone out. "Good news. My uncle says the developers got the variance approved. The Hathaway tract. Four hundred units."

"Four hundred." She was still holding the library book.

"Housing crisis, remember. People need places to live." He said it the way people say things they've decided not to think about. Devon's father sold insurance to the construction companies; Katherine had never held that against him until she noticed she was starting to.

In fifth period the group met in the corner of the classroom. Priya had printed aquifer maps, which was more than anyone expected. "The recharge zone runs right under the Hathaway tract," Priya said, tapping the paper. "More houses, more wells, more pavement. Rain doesn't soak in through pavement."

"So we draw a picture of pavement," Devon said. "Failing grade, guaranteed."

Katherine opened the book between them. "In 1972 these MIT people ran this whole world through a computer. Population, food, industry, pollution, resources, all linked. It was for the Club of Rome. The model was called World3."

"What did it say?" Priya asked.

"That's the part I'm still reading." That wasn't quite true. She had read the conclusions twice the night before, but saying them out loud felt like claiming something she hadn't earned yet. The MIT team had linked everything, and linking everything meant you couldn't pull one thread without the others moving. She didn't know yet what that meant for a town of eleven thousand with one aquifer.

That evening she went to her grandmother's house, because her grandmother had lived here when the reservoir was built and because her mother had said, twice, that Katherine should. Her grandmother was on the porch shelling peas.

"Did you know the reservoir almost didn't happen?" her grandmother said. "The farmers expostulated for a year. Letters to the paper, meetings at the grange. Then the drought came, and the letters stopped." She dropped peas into the bowl. "Everything here comes from that water. This town's whole lineage, you might say. Your grandfather's mill, the school, this house."

Katherine turned that over. She had been thinking of the water supply as one box on a poster and the growth as another box. But the book hadn't used boxes. It had used links, arrows that ran both ways. More industry drew more people, more people needed more food and more water, more of everything made more pollution, and pollution and resources pushed back on all of it. The town was small, but it wasn't separate. The developers needed buyers, the buyers needed jobs, the jobs were mostly at the distribution center out by the highway, and the highway had been built with federal money, which meant the growth was not exactly the town's own decision. Some of the pressure was extrinsic, she thought, coming from outside, like weather.

"You're quiet," her grandmother said.

"I'm working on something." Katherine picked up a pea pod and split it badly, crushing two peas.

On Thursday night the group met at Priya's kitchen table. Priya had made a spreadsheet: households, projected gallons per day, aquifer recharge rates she'd gotten from a county website. Devon had, unexpectedly, brought the sale price of the new units. "Two bedrooms starting at four hundred grand," he said. "My dad says half the buyers will commute to the city." He looked at Priya's numbers, then at his own, and for a second his face did something complicated. "Nobody making our town's wages can buy those."

Katherine spread the map, the spreadsheet, and the library book across the table. "Okay. So here's what I want to try. The MIT book linked things. Population, food, industry, pollution, resources. That was the whole world, but the idea works small. Watch." She drew the aquifer in pencil. She drew an arrow to the new development, an arrow back from pavement to runoff, an arrow from the distribution center to the jobs that justified the development, an arrow from the city's housing prices to the buyers. "Every line goes two ways. Pull here, something moves there."

They worked until eleven. Priya argued that recharge was the choke point; Devon argued that if they killed the development the jobs died too, and the town's school was already losing funding. They were both right, Katherine realized, which was the problem the book had been having since 1972.

On Friday Mr. Reyes walked the rows slowly. When he reached their table he stopped, put on his glasses, and read the web of arrows for a long time. "Where's this from?"

"A model called World3," Katherine said. "MIT. 1972. It was done for the Club of Rome. We shrank it."

He tapped the arrow between the distribution center and the buyers. "And this link. How confident are you in this one?"

"About sixty percent," Katherine said.

Devon exhaled through his teeth. Priya grinned. Mr. Reyes wrote something in his binder, and Katherine watched the pencil move, and did not look away.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: Automation bias is the tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct.
story:
The espresso machine had been hissing for two years before the tablet arrived, and Isla still thought of the tablet as a guest that had refused to leave. It decided who worked which shift, ranked the regulars by "loyalty score," and, as of Monday, flagged transactions it considered suspicious. Her manager, Dev, trusted it the way some people trusted weather reports more than the sky.

Mrs. Okafor came in at quarter past eight, which was itself seismic, because she had come at eight sharp every morning for a decade. Her coat was damp and one shoe was ruined. "The GPS took me down Hollow Creek Road," she said, setting her umbrella in the stand with its usual mannerism, handle turned outward, as though nothing had happened. "There were cones. A sign that said closed. But the voice kept saying left in two hundred feet, so I went left."

"You went around the cones?" Isla asked, already pouring the medium drip Mrs. Okafor never had to order.

"Between them, really. Very smoothly. Then the road stopped being a road." She said it lightly, but her hand shook a little on the cup. "The voice was so confident. It seemed wrong to disobey it."

Isla had a twenty-minute gap before the morning rush, so she stood by the pastry case with her phone and searched "why do people follow GPS onto closed roads." The top result was a short article with a name for it. She read it twice, then said it out loud, mostly to the croissants. "Automation bias. The tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct." The cones had been correct. The sign had been correct. Mrs. Okafor had a wet shoe anyway.

She was still holding that thought when Dana came in from the loading dock, waving her own phone. The tablet had rejected Dana's shift swap, the one Isla had approved on paper Sunday, because the system "detected an anomalous pattern of schedule manipulation." Dana had worked every one of those swapped shifts. She had the shifts' worth of dry hands and desiccated fingertips from the dish sprayer to prove it. Dev had looked at the paper schedule, looked at the tablet's red flag, and sided with the tablet. "It cross-references things we can't see," he'd said. Isla had pointed out that what they could see was Dana, standing there, having worked. Dev had tapped the screen gently, like patting a dog with a badge.

Now Isla counted on her fingers, out loud, so Dana could hear the tally: the cones Mrs. Okafor drove past, the paper schedule Dev overrode, and last month, the camera over the register that had auto-flagged the tip jar count and got Tomas written up for eleven dollars that turned out to be in the safe, exactly where he'd logged it. Three for the machines, zero for the contradicting information, which kept being correct and kept losing. She wasn't against the tablet. It caught actual theft sometimes; it scheduled around exams nobody remembered to mention; it never called in sick. But she noticed she had started believing it by default, the way Dev did, and that felt less like a decision than a slow leak.

She took the paper schedule and the tablet's rejection notice and laid both on the counter in front of Dev. "One of these is a machine that can't see Dana," she said. "The other is Dana's actual hours with my signature. You don't have to pick the paper. Just look at both before you pick." Dev picked up the paper, then put it down, then picked it up again, which for Dev was practically a conversion experience. He re-approved the swap with a note in the log. The tablet would probably flag it again by Thursday. Isla was honest enough, with herself anyway, to admit she didn't know what to do about that part, about systems that made you argue with them twice.

Mrs. Okafor finished her coffee and gathered the ruined shoe business into her coat like a folded map. At the door she paused. "Tomorrow I'm taking Ellsworth," she said. "It's six minutes longer and the voice hates it. Let it sulk."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
Her father's car had a smell of pencil shavings and old coffee, and the instructor, a square woman named Mrs. Okafor, sat in the passenger seat and did not touch the key.

"Belt," she said.

Alexia had already put her hands on the wheel at ten and two, exactly as the booklet showed, and had adjusted the mirror, and had announced "checking mirrors" in the flat voice of someone checking mirrors. The belt had simply not occurred to her. She reached for it now, and the buckle clicked, and Mrs. Okafor turned the key as though nothing had happened, though Alexia suspected that something had, the way a first point is lost without anyone saying the score.

They pulled out of the gravel drive and onto the county road, which ran straight between soybean fields until it forgot itself near the creek. It was the second week of August, and her father was away on sabbatical, which was a word he used to mean a year in Tucson cataloguing lichens, and which her mother used to mean that someone else would have to teach Alexia to drive. Hence Mrs. Okafor, hence the insurance forms Alexia had signed in the kitchen, one clause of which promised to indemnify the driving school against anything Alexia did to a fence, a mailbox, or a passing cow. She had read it twice. It was the most adult thing she had ever signed.

"Relax your thumbs," Mrs. Okafor said. "You're strangling the wheel."

At the stop sign at Fenwick Road, Alexia stopped, checked both ways twice, and then sat there while a red-tailed hawk crossed the road at its leisure. She was thinking about the belt. Not the buckle, but the statistic printed in the margin of the driver's manual, next to a drawing of a skeleton wearing a shoulder harness like a pageant sash. Her friend Devi, who wanted to be an epidemiologist and said so at parties, had once recited it over cafeteria pizza: according to the CDC, wearing a seat belt cuts serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. Devi had called not wearing one "pernicious," which Alexia had looked up afterward, mostly to check whether Devi was using it correctly. She had been.

Half. Alexia turned onto Fenwick and accelerated to forty, then forty-five, then a cautious thirty-eight. Half was a strange number to hold in your head while steering. It was not a promise, the way her grandmother's prayers were promises, and it was not nothing, the way her cousin Ren treated every safety measure as an insult to his constitution. It was something in between, a probability, and she found she didn't know what to do with probabilities except carry them.

The summer she was eleven, before Ren had his motorcycle, her uncle had taken her and Ren out on this same road in his truck, and Ren had refused the belt on the grounds that he was eleven and free. Her uncle had refused to start the engine, and the two of them had sat in a parked truck in the August heat for forty minutes, both grinning, both certain the other would fold. Alexia, sweating in the back with her own belt on, had watched a spider build half a web on the windshield and had admired them both: her uncle for the principle, Ren for the stubbornness, though she understood even then that only one of them was going to grow up to be the sort of person who insisted.

"What's your speed?" Mrs. Okafor asked.

"Thirty-eight."

"Forty's fine here. You don't have to atone for the whole road."

Alexia eased up to forty. The creek came and went on the left, and the soybeans gave way to corn, and she understood something small and unsatisfying, which was that she agreed with her uncle and not with Ren, and also that she couldn't prove him right, exactly. Half. Not all, not none. Belt on, keys turn. That was the whole of her philosophy so far, and it seemed, for a first lesson, like enough.

"Turn here," Mrs. Okafor said. "Use your signal."

Alexia flicked the lever, checked the mirror, and made the widest turn of her life, both hands still on the wheel, the belt lying warm across her chest like a hand that had been there all along.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 2011 the OPERA experiment reported neutrinos apparently faster than light; in 2012 the result was traced to a loose fibre-optic cable, and other experiments measured speeds consistent with light.
story:
The waiting room had four chairs and a fish tank with a single angelfish circling a plastic plant, and Lauren had memorized its route by the time her name was called. She was here for the second set of bloodwork. The first set had come back with something the receptionist wouldn't describe over the phone, only an "idiosyncrasy" in her clotting numbers, which was the word the nurse had used, the sort of word that meant nothing and therefore everything. Lauren wanted a clean result by Friday, because Friday was the deadline to confirm her spot on the summer research trip, three weeks on a boat studying pelagic birds off Cape Cod, the first thing she had ever wanted that required someone else's signature.

Her mother sat beside her with her coat folded over her knees. While they waited, Lauren's phone buzzed. A message from Dana, all capitals: HAVE YOU SEEN THIS. Below it, a link with a headline about an experiment that had proven Einstein wrong, particles traveling faster than light. Dana's next message read, physics is fake, everything they taught us is fake, and Lauren smiled at the screen the way you smile at a friend who is wrong with total confidence.

She looked up at the fish, then back down. Faster than light. She had a vague memory of her physics teacher mentioning it, but vaguely, and Dana's headline was new, or looked new. There was a poster in the doctor's hallway about not trusting medical advice from the internet, and Lauren thought about that while she typed OPERA neutrinos faster than light into the search bar, then deleted it and typed the headline itself, which was less leading, though she wasn't sure why that mattered yet.

The results assembled themselves slowly, the way silt coagulates at the bottom of a glass. In 2011, an experiment called OPERA had reported neutrinos that seemed to arrive faster than light. Seemed. Other labs had gone looking for the same thing and not found it. And in 2012, the OPERA result itself had been traced to a loose fibre-optic cable. Lauren read the sentence twice, then a third time. One cable. Other experiments, measuring again, had found the neutrinos moving at speeds consistent with light. So nothing had overturned anything; one team's anomaly had dissolved into a mechanical fault, and the checks that dissolved it were, she realized, the whole point. Nobody had believed the first number just because it was a number.

"Lauren," the nurse called, and she put the phone away.

They took her into the small room, and her blood pressure was fine, her pulse was fine, and the doctor came in with a folder and said the second panel had partially corrected the first. One marker was now normal. Another was still borderline, and there was a third test, a confirmatory one, that took ten days to process. Ten days. The trip left in twelve. Lauren did the arithmetic instantly and felt her stomach drop through the floor of the small room.

Her mother watched her daughter's face while the doctor talked, and what she saw there she recognized from the day Lauren had fallen off her bike at nine and stood up slowly, checking for damage before deciding whether to cry. The girl was doing that now, running some interior calculation about what she could still salvage. Her mother wanted to say that the trip would come again next summer, and knew exactly how that would land, as if next summer were a reasonable substitute for the only summer in which Lauren was seventeen and accepted and packed. So instead she said, "Can we do the blood draw today?" and watched her daughter's shoulders lower half an inch.

"Yes, today's fine," the doctor said, already writing the order, and then, almost as an aside, "I'd rather re-run it than trust one panel. That's how we get to something true in this business." Lauren nodded, and in the drawing chair, with the tourniquet biting her arm, she texted Dana back: it was OPERA in 2011, but in 2012 they traced it to a loose cable, and the other experiments matched light. One weird result isn't a discovery. Dana replied with a single eye-roll emoji and the words okay einstein, and Lauren laughed once, quietly, while the needle went in.

The vial filled dark and quick, and the nurse labeled it and set it in the rack with the others. Ten days, twelve until the boat. The angelfish was still circling its plastic plant when they passed back through the waiting room, tracing the same loop it had traced all morning, as if repetition were the only way it knew to be sure of anything. Lauren stopped at the window and looked out at the parking lot, then at her phone, at Dana's message still on the screen. "Book the trip," her mother said behind her. "We'll call them Friday."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Biotech billionaire Patrick Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for $500 million, plus the assumption of pension obligations.
story:
The library's study room smelled like dry-erase marker and the cafeteria pizza Marcus had smuggled in behind the copy machine. Owen spread his sources across the table: two newspapers, a laptop with a dying battery, and the debate outline he was supposed to finish by Friday. The resolution was "A free press requires independent ownership," and Owen had drawn the negative, which meant he had to argue that rich owners could save newspapers instead of ruining them. His father, over rice and burnt chicken on Tuesday, had pounded the table about it. "Nobody buys a sinking ship out of charity," his father had said, while his mother said the ship was sinking anyway and somebody had to buy it, and his sister asked if she could be excused.

Owen had come to the library to find out which parent was right. He typed the name his father had dropped like a card on the table: Patrick Soon-Shiong, the biotech billionaire. The database loaded slowly, the way everything loaded when you had twenty minutes of Wi-Fi and a charger someone had already borrowed. The first result said Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for $500 million. Owen wrote that down. Then he kept reading and found the rest, the part his father hadn't mentioned: he also took on the pension obligations, the money owed to the paper's retired workers.

"Five hundred million," Marcus said, reading over his shoulder. "Plus pensions. That's like buying a house and also agreeing to pay the previous owner's mom's rent forever."

"That's the point, though," Owen said. "The pensions are the expensive part. Anybody could write a check for the building."

Marcus pulled a chair around and sat backward on it, arms folded across the backrest, which he did whenever he wanted to argue without admitting he wanted to argue. "So he's either a saint or a puppet master. Pick one, you have a debate to win."

The trouble was that Owen could see the shape of both arguments at once, and neither one fit inside the other. He found a story from after the sale, reporters describing the newsroom's fear that a billionaire's businesses, his drugs, his hospitals, his lawsuits, might quietly become untouchable in the paper's own pages. Then he found a story about editors pushing back on the owner over a planned endorsement, and the paper's editorial board overriding it. Both stories were in papers owned by other companies, which meant other owners, which meant the mirror went all the way down. Owen wrote a question mark in his margin and hated how accurate it was.

"You're spiraling," Marcus said. "It's a debate, not a religion. You just have to sound right for eight minutes."

"That's the problem with you," Owen said. "You think arguments are costumes." Marcus looked wounded, then stole a slice of the pizza, which was his way of accepting the insult.

Owen tried a different shelf, the periodicals, and found an old issue of the Los Angeles Times itself, printed months after the sale. He flipped to the business section and there it was, an article about one of Soon-Shiong's companies, written in the flat, unflattered tone of a paper covering somebody it could not afford to flatter. Or was the flatness itself the disguise? He held the page up to the light as though bias might be visible there, a watermark of ownership, and felt stupid doing it, and did it anyway.

His father had said, at dinner, "Money is never neutral." His mother had said, "Nothing is neutral, honey, that's not a standard, that's a mood." Owen had laughed then. Now, in the study room, he underlined his own outline, where he'd written that independence is a practice rather than a bank account, reporters who challenge their owner are independent the way a muscle is strong, by use, not by birth, and he wondered if that was an argument or a wish dressed in an argument's clothes. In English class they'd just finished a unit on existentialism, the idea that you are what you do, moment by moment, with no essence underneath to guarantee you. He'd thought it was depressing. Applied to a newspaper it was almost hopeful: no owner, however rich, could settle the question once, because the question came back with every story, every day, and had to be answered again by people who could choose badly or choose well.

He tried to suture the two halves of his outline together, the praise and the worry, and the line held, mostly. A newspaper saved by a billionaire is still a newspaper whose survival depends on one man's patience. A newspaper closed for lack of one is not independent either, it's gone. Somewhere between those sentences was his actual position, and it refused to sit still long enough for him to write it down cleanly, which he suspected meant it was the honest one.

Marcus leaned over and read the new paragraph. "So which side are you arguing Friday?"

"Mine," Owen said.

"That's not a side."

"Then I'll lose." Owen closed the laptop, slid the old Times into his backpack with the care of someone borrowing something he intended to return, and looked at the clock. His mother would want the whole story at dinner, and his father would push his rice around and say, "Nobody buys a sinking ship out of charity." Owen stood, chair scraping, and Marcus said, "Tell them I said hi," and Owen was already through the doors, out into the alluvial light of late afternoon, the low sun spreading gold across the parking lot like sediment, deciding on the drive home exactly which sentence he would open with.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A guitar in standard tuning has its six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, to E, A, D, G, B and E.
story:
The studio smelled of lemon polish and cold coffee, and the guitar lying across Sara's knees was not the nylon-string loaner she'd been using all spring. It was her grandfather's, a dreadnought with a sunburst finish gone amber at the edges, and it had spent eleven years in a closet in Paramus before her mother dug it out and said, take it, he'd want it played.

"Standard tuning," Mr. Okonkwo said, tapping the tuning pegs one by one. "From the lowest string to the highest, that's E, A, D, G, B, E." He plucked the fattest string and it wobbled flat, a sour moan, and he raised his eyebrows at her as if to say, your inheritance, your problem.

She had assumed the guitar would come to her ready. That was the first small insult of the afternoon: nothing arrives tuned. Her grandfather, she remembered suddenly, had sat on his porch in August with this same instrument across his belly, sweating through his shirt, turning a peg in tiny patient increments while the cicadas screamed. She had been nine and had asked why he kept doing the same thing over and over. "Because it drifts," he'd said. "Everything drifts, Saraleh." Then he'd played something Balkan-sounding and crooked, nothing like the chords she would later learn, and she had gone inside for ice, unimpressed.

Now she turned the lowest peg herself and watched Mr. Okonkwo's clip-on tuner, a little green-eyed parasite on the headstock. The needle swam left. Too low. She tightened, overshot, backed off. E. Then A, then D, each string a negotiation between her ear, which was mostly guesswork, and the needle, which was merciless. When she reached the fourth string and plucked, the tuner read F. She stared at it, plucked again, and Mr. Okonkwo laughed, actually laughed, the sound bouncing off the acoustic foam panels.

"Whoever restrung this put the G where a B ought to live," he said. "Or you've invented a new tuning. Groucho Marx had one, you know. Ask your grandfather."

"He's dead," Sara said, and then, because his face did the thing faces do, "eleven years. It's fine. Tell me about Groucho."

So she had to restring it, or at least detune and retune across the confusion, working out which string was which by listening down from the low E she'd already set: E, A, D, then G, then B, then the thin high E, and she said the sequence aloud like a spell, and Mr. Okonkwo made her say it again without looking at the tuner. Her fingertips hurt within twenty minutes, the old calluses from the loaner being the wrong kind, too soft in the wrong places. That was the arrangement with the guitar, apparently. It would let her learn it, but it charged interest.

Here was the thing she couldn't decide, and she told him so while she worked the B string up to pitch: part of her wanted the guitar tuned exactly, note-perfect, the way the tuner demanded, because that was the contract of music and because her grandfather had clearly believed in it, all that porch-side drifting-and-correcting. But another part of her kept thinking about his crooked Balkan tune, which had probably been out of tune by every objective measure and had still, in her memory, transfigured a hot boring afternoon into something she could still hear fourteen years later. Perfection versus that. She couldn't get them into the same sentence without cheating.

"It's not a plebiscite," Mr. Okonkwo said when she tried to frame it as two camps, the tuners and the drifters, and asked which side won. "You don't get to vote once and be done. You tune it every single time you pick it up. Every time. That's the whole job." He said it lightly, but she felt the weight land anyway, some of it unfair, some of it hers to carry.

By the end of the hour she had all six strings right, E to E, the way he'd said at the start, and she played an open chord, a clumsy C, and the sound was enormous in the little room, pelagic, like something deep surfacing. Mr. Okonkwo nodded once and started stacking his sheet music, which was how she knew the lesson was over and that it had gone well. She loosened the strings a quarter turn each, the way you're supposed to when you're done, and felt stupid about it, undoing the hour on purpose. At the door she stopped. "Is it cheating if I record myself saying it and listen on the bus? E, A, D, G, B, E." He looked up, considering. "It's cheating," he said, "if you never stop needing the recording."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, the US unemployment rate was 3.9 percent for workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma and 5.6 percent for those without one.
story:
The parking lot had been striped for graduation since Monday, and by Saturday afternoon the white lines were already flaking under two hundred folding chairs. Sofia stood beside her mother's Corolla in her gown, which was, according to the tag, "one size fits most," a maxim she intended to test by sitting down without splitting anything. She had the cap in one hand and her phone in the other, checking the time not because it mattered but because checking the time was something to do with her hands.

Marcus was leaning against the chain-link at the far edge of the lot, still in his work shirt from the warehouse, still holding the energy drink he'd been holding since junior year, it seemed. He had dropped out eighteen months ago, and they had not exactly stopped being friends so much as stopped being in the same building. She crossed the lot before she could decide whether to.

"So you did it," he said. "They let you walk."

"They let everyone walk. That's the whole point of the ceremony."

"Congratulations, I guess." He gesticulated with the can, a small ironic wave, and she noticed the ink on his forearm, a date she didn't recognize. "I've been putting in applications. Fourteen since March. I got one interview, at the tire place, and the guy asked if I had my diploma and I said I was working on the GED and he sort of nodded like that was a nice thing I'd said about the weather."

She wanted to say something useful. She was, in general, the person who said useful things; her friends had pointed this out often enough that it had stopped being a compliment. "I looked some of this up," she said, "for my econ paper. Last year, unemployment for people twenty-five and older with a high school diploma was 3.9 percent. Without one, 5.6."

"Where'd you find that?"

"Bureau of Labor Statistics. I had to cite everything, Mrs. Ahn was ruthless."

"So it's not that bad either way," Marcus said. "Sixteen people out of a hundred without a diploma, that's still a lot of jobs."

"Four point a half," she said. "Out of a hundred. Five point six." She heard herself doing the arithmetic out loud and stopped, but he had already shrugged, which was his way of filing things.

Her mother had a position on all this, delivered over the years with the confidence of someone who had once read half an article: school was the door, and without it you were outside knocking. Sofia had absorbed the position the way she'd absorbed the family recipes, without examination, and had repeated it in her college essay, "education as threshold," a phrase she now found slightly embarrassing. But the numbers she'd found herself were quieter than her mother's version. They said something smaller and harder to argue with, something about margins and odds rather than doors, and she hadn't fully worked out what she thought a margin obligated a person to do, or whether odds were the same thing as fairness.

There was a flashback she kept returning to, unbidden, at moments like this one. Sophomore year, before he'd stopped coming, Marcus had stayed after fifth period to help her jump the Corolla, because she'd left the lights on again, and he'd known exactly which terminal to clamp and in what order, and he'd explained it without making her feel stupid, which almost no one managed. "Red is positive," he'd said. "Dead battery first. It's not hard, people just like pretending it is." She had felt, that afternoon in the student lot with the hood propped and the November light going gray, that there were kinds of knowing she would never have, and that this was not a tragedy, just a fact with a shape.

"Hey," she said now. "The GED. Are you actually doing it?"

"Doing the practice tests. Math's fine. The essay part wants me to argue one side of something, which, you know me."

"I do know you." She laughed. "You'd argue both sides and fail for hedging."

"They should give extra credit for that," Marcus said. "Some of us can see the whole parking lot."

The PA crackled somewhere near the gym, the muffled voice telling seniors to line up. Sofia pulled at her gown, and a seam held, and she filed this under victories. She did not say the thing she had drafted, which was that the numbers meant he should finish, because the numbers did not exactly mean that; they meant his life would be one and a half someones harder in a way no one could point to on a calendar, and she could not honestly promise that a certificate would fix the tire place, or anything else. What she had instead was the memory of him explaining the jumper cables, patient, competent, undeservedly confident in her ability to turn a key.

"I'll sit with my phone on," she said, pulling on the cap. "Text me if the essay thing defeats you. I've written enough dishonest one-sided arguments for both of us."

"The ceremony's an hour," Marcus said. "That's a long time to keep a phone on."

"I'm graduating, not dying." She started toward the gym doors, gown flapping, one hand holding the cap down against a gust that came from nowhere, the way gusts in that lot always did.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
story:
Anais had promised herself she would finish the portrait before Sunday, and now it was Friday afternoon and her grandmother's kitchen smelled of turpentine and toast. The portrait was of her grandmother at sixty, copied from a photograph she had found in the hallway drawer: her grandmother leaning on a gate in a yellow dress, squinting into some summer that had happened before Anais was born. She had it half done on the canvas propped against the salt jar, the left side tender and finished, the right side still raw pencil lines.

"I don't squint like that," her grandmother said, coming in with the shopping.

"You do. You do it at crossword clues."

"Nonsense. I look at things squarely. I'm a pragmatist." She set down the bags and studied the canvas for a long moment, and Anais could not tell whether the look was criticism or being moved, or both, which with her grandmother was often the case.

Anais was painting with the acrylics her uncle had left in the spare room years ago, tubes with names like Hooker's Green and Yellow Ochre, half of them crusted at the mouth. She had discovered on Wednesday that the paint thinned beautifully under the tap, that it moved like watercolor when she wanted it to, spreading in soft river deltas down the paper. That was how she had done the left side, all pale washes, and it looked like memory itself. She was proud of it in a way she did not say out loud.

But the right side wanted something else. In the photograph her grandmother's hands were gripping the gate, knuckles sharp, and every time Anais tried to wash them in like the rest, they dissolved into vagueness, into a grandmother-shaped blur. The hands needed to be solid. She wanted them opaque and stubborn, paint laid on thick, so that anyone looking would know those hands had held onto things.

She mixed a flesh tone in the jar lid and worked for an hour, then went out to the garden because Tom next door was calling something through the hedge about the wasps. She stayed longer than she meant to, arguing about whether the nest was theirs to remove or the council's, and when she came back the light had gone slanted and her brushes stood in the jar like little burnt trees. The bristles were stiff as matchsticks. She took one to the tap and ran hot water over it and bent it and the hairs snapped rather than softened, and when she tried to scrub the dried paint from the palette it sat there, glazed and insolent, refusing the water entirely.

She sat down on the kitchen floor, peevish, holding the ruined brush. So that was the arrangement: the paint was water-based while wet, it answered her completely, and then it dried, quickly, without ceremony, and after that it was water-resistant, past persuasion. She thought about her father, who had said at Christmas that painting was a lovely hobby but that she should think about something that would emancipate her, by which he seemed to mean a career that would let her leave. He had a washable kind of hope for her, one that rinsed out when it dried. She turned the brush over in her fingers. There was another jar in the spare room, and a bundle of new brushes still in their packet, and she thought she understood something, though she could not have said it in a sentence: that a thing could start soft and end permanent, and that this was not a betrayal of the softness but the whole point of it. Or possibly not. Possibly she was only justifying a mess.

She brought the fresh brushes down and unscrewed a new tube. The right side she would paint fast and thick, deciding each stroke before it left the bristle, because she would not get to reconsider it once it dried. The left side would stay as it was, pale and unfinished, water still implied in it. Her grandmother came in and stood at her shoulder.

"One half fog and one half fence post," her grandmother said. "Is that deliberate?"

"I don't know yet," said Anais, dipping the brush. "Ask me when it's dry."
