story:
The line at First Meridian had six people in it and Lily counted them twice, because counting was easier than deciding. Her grandmother had claimed two chairs by the desk with the rope barrier, saving spots the way she saved spots at church, with her purse on one seat and her cane across the other. Lily sat down with the canvas bag in her lap and did not open it.

Marco was already at the desk, turning a statement sideways as though the numbers would rearrange themselves into something kinder. He was twenty-four, he had a wife and a baby on the way, and in three weeks he was supposed to close on a small house on Delancey Street. Lily had heard her grandmother on the phone all week, historicizing the whole affair, placing it in a long line of family milestones: Uncle Sal's storefront in 1974, her own first flat after the war, every relative who had ever signed anything at a bank with the whole family watching. "We are a polity of homeowners," she liked to say, though Lily suspected most polities did not hold meetings over cannoli.

"There's a charge here I don't understand," Marco said to the loan officer, a woman named Priya whose badge was pinned slightly crooked. He slid the paper across. "Every month, on top of the payment. Almost two hundred dollars."

Priya tapped the line. "You put five percent down," she said. "Below twenty, on a conventional mortgage, that carries private mortgage insurance."

"It protects the lender, not the buyer," Lily's grandmother said from the chairs, not unkindly, the way she might identify a bird. Marco looked at her, then back at Priya, who nodded once and reached for another form.

Lily sat very still. She was thinking about the apartment on Rankin Street, the one she and Dana had toured in April, third floor, a radiator that clanked like applause. The landlord wanted first month, last month, and a security deposit, which Dana had explained meant three rents upfront and none of it coming back if you broke anything. Eleven hundred a month, times three. Lily had done that math on the bus so many times the figures wore grooves. Rent, Dana said, was money you burned to keep warm; a mortgage was money you kept. Lily had found that neat and suspicious, the way slogans usually were.

The summer before, she had worked the counter at Corso's Deli, forty hours a week, and her grandmother had paid her under the table for painting the porch, and there had been the graduation cards, ten and twenty dollars folded into their little envelopes. She had kept it in a shoebox and then, when the shoebox felt childish, in a savings account with a passbook so thin it embarrassed her. This morning she had withdrawn all of it and put the envelope in the canvas bag, and she had told no one, not even Dana, what it was for. That was the thing she could not decide, and the teller line moved forward one person, and it did not help at all.

Priya was laying it out for Marco with a yellow highlighter. His closing costs had come in higher than the estimate, the seller had refused to cover the inspection repairs, and the five percent he had scraped together was suddenly, equivocally, not quite enough. Not a refusal. Not an approval. A number on a page that had moved. "If the down payment shrinks any further," Priya said, "the monthly insurance goes up. If it grows, the picture changes."

Lily stood up. She crossed the carpet that everyone in her family had crossed at one time or another, and she set the canvas bag on the edge of Marco's desk, and she took out the envelope. Thirty-one hundred dollars, mostly in twenties, the deli's smell still in the bills. "For the down payment," she said. Her voice came out steadier than she expected. "It's a gift. I signed something about that once, at the deli, when Mr. Corso's daughter bought the truck."

Marco stared at the envelope. Priya looked at Lily over her glasses and asked how old she was, and Lily said eighteen, and Priya said that was fine as long as there was a gift letter, and pulled a blank sheet toward her. "This gets you to about nine percent," she told Marco. "The insurance stays on, but it drops."

"Rent money," Lily said, mostly to herself. "I was going to use it for rent."

Her grandmother had come to stand behind them both, purse first. She looked at the envelope, then at Lily, for a long moment, and whatever she was calculating she kept to herself. Marco reached across and put his hand flat on the envelope, the way you steady something that might blow away.

"You sure?" he said.

Lily looked at the yellow lines on the page, at the house on Delancey Street that she had never seen, at the little crooked badge on Priya's blouse.

"Count it," she said.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Most US employment is at-will, meaning the employer or the worker can end the job at any time for any reason that is not illegal.
story:
The notice went up on Monday, tacked to the corkboard beside the lost-and-found bin: waterfront staff needed for the last four weeks of camp, applicants must be sixteen by June, interviews Friday at noon. Kaitlyn had been a CIT all summer, unpaid, hauling coolers and counting noses on the dock while the lifeguards sat in their tower and got paid to whistle. She wanted the tower. She wanted the tower so badly she had practiced her rescue breathing on a pillow the night before, timing herself, thirty compressions, thirty again.

But on Wednesday her phone buzzed at lunch. Marguerite, who ran the gift shop at the lake marina two towns over, needed someone for the rest of the season, starting Monday, eleven dollars an hour, cash tips on Saturdays. The camp job paid a stipend, a flat four hundred for four weeks, which worked out to less. Kaitlyn did the math twice on the back of a permission slip, then sat very still while a nine-year-old asked her to open his juice box.

"You already said yes to Marguerite?" Priya asked her that evening at the picnic tables, where the staff ate after the campers went home. Priya was seventeen and knew things the way she knew the periodic table, thoroughly and with citations.

"I said I'd come by tomorrow to fill out paperwork. She wants an answer before Saturday. But if I get the waterfront job Friday, and then the marina's better, I'd be quitting the camp job. I can't do that to them. They trained me. There's, like, four weeks left."

"So don't apply."

"Then if I don't get the marina paperwork done by Saturday, I have nothing."

Priya peeled the label off her water bottle in one long strip. "My cousin quit Kroger with a text message the night before her shift. No notice at all. She said it's called at-will. Most employment in the US is at-will, so the employer or the worker can end the job at any time, for any reason that isn't illegal. Kroger could've fired her that same way. Nobody's more wronged than anybody."

"That feels like a loophole," Kaitlyn said. "Like finding a rule that exonerates you before you've even done the thing."

"It's not a loophole if it's the whole road."

Kaitlyn didn't answer. Over by the fence, Mr. Deene, the program director, stood watching the empty swim area with his hands clasped behind him, saturnine in the long orange light, the way he always looked at the end of a day, as though tallying what had gone wrong. He had driven her to get her CPR card renewed himself, in his own car, and had waited in the parking lot reading a paperback. That was the problem with people. They kept doing things you'd have to remember later.

On Thursday she took her charges to the nature hut, where the quiet CIT, a college sophomore named Devon, was helping kids extract DNA from strawberries. Kaitlyn's least favorite camper, a boy named Oliver, mashed his strawberry with unusual violence and then peered into the bag. "So this is his genotype?" he asked, pointing at the goop. "The whole blueprint?"

"That's his DNA," Devon said. "The genotype's more like the instructions written in it. You can't see the instructions, only what they build."

Oliver squinted, unsatisfied, and went back to mashing. Kaitlyn stood there with a sudden clear picture of herself: instructions nobody could see, and a person built on top of them, and no way to know if the person matched. She believed she was loyal. She had a wallet card and a four-week record of punctual cooler-hauling to prove it. But the instructions, the ones you couldn't see, might just say take the eleven dollars an hour, and she'd never had them tested.

Friday at noon she sat across the picnic table from Mr. Deene, who had her file open even though there was almost nothing in it. He asked her the questions, she answered them, and then he said, "You'd start Monday. I have to tell you, though, if enrollment drops I cut staff the same week. It's the nature of the arrangement. Nothing personal, it's just how it works. I'd let you go with a day's notice if it came to that."

She looked at him. "So the camp could end it any time."

"That's the deal," he said, and closed the file. "I'd tell you the truth about that much."

He had not known he was doing it, but he had tipped the scale, or maybe he had only shown her where the scale already sat. The camp could cut her loose on a day's notice because that was the arrangement, ordinary and legal, and Priya's cousin could quit Kroger by text under the same arrangement, and neither one was a betrayal. Or both were, a little, and the arrangement just spread the small betrayals evenly so nobody had to carry one alone. She could not decide which way to see it. What she knew was that she would not be the only one at the picnic table with obligations.

"The waterfront's yours if you want it," Mr. Deene said. "I need an answer before the staff meeting at five."

"I know. I'll be back by four thirty."

She rode her bike the two miles to the marina with the permission-slip math folded in her pocket. Marguerite had her filling out the W-4 under the ceiling fan, then held out a pen for the schedule. "Monday through Saturday, nine to five. You're sure? I'm training you on the register and I don't get a second shot at the season."

"I'm sure about the job," Kaitlyn said. "I'm not sure about the money being the reason. Does that count?"

Marguerite considered her over the counter, the way she probably considered weather. "Counts more than the other kind," she said. "The sure ones quit by August."

At four twenty-five Kaitlyn stood at the edge of the staff meeting with the wind coming off the lake. Mr. Deene raised his eyebrows at her from the circle of folding chairs.

"I'm taking the marina job," she said. "And I'll finish out this week, today and tomorrow, the full days, so you're not short at the swim test." She held out her CPR card, since there was nothing else to give him. "I can't give you four weeks' notice. I'm sorry. I looked it up and I don't legally owe any, but that part I already knew before I looked."

Mr. Deene took the card, turned it over once, and handed it back. "Saturday, then," he said. "Bring the whistles back to the tower."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Roger Tomlinson led development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s, the first computerized GIS, and is often called the father of GIS.
story:
The travel agency occupied the ground floor of a building that had once been a bank, and Gabriel sat at the teller counter where his mother had arranged for him to help Mr. Adeyemi update the shop's wall maps before he left for university. The summer job was meant to be dull. Instead Mr. Adeyemi had installed a trial of mapping software on the back computer and told him, almost as an afterthought, that the city council had published flood risk data and that anyone could now lay it over a map of neighborhoods. Gabriel had assumed floods were a rural problem, something that happened to farms and river towns, and the assumption collapsed the first time he clicked the overlay button and watched the blue shading bloom across the eastern districts of the city he had lived in for eighteen years.

He learned the software the way he learned most things, by breaking it and starting over. Layers, he discovered, could be stacked like transparencies on an old projector: streets beneath parcels, parcels beneath the floodplain polygon, and above everything a census layer showing which blocks held the oldest housing. When he switched the layers on and off, the city changed its mind about itself. The same streets that looked ordinary under the street layer looked fragile under the flood layer, and the houses his aunt rented in Marshview sat squarely inside the deepest blue.

"You've been at that machine for three hours," Mr. Adeyemi said on the second Thursday, carrying two cups of tea though Gabriel drank coffee. "My customers think we've become an internet café."

"It's a GIS," Gabriel said. "A geographic information system. You put different kinds of data on one map and look at them together." He turned the monitor so the older man could see the blue and the census blocks overlapping. "This whole technology started in Canada. Roger Tomlinson led the development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s. First computerized one there ever was. They call him the father of GIS."

Mr. Adeyemi leaned in, reading the screen the way he read timetables, with a finger tracking the lines. "And this flood layer, is it a guess?"

"It's a model," Gabriel said, and then, because he had spent two evenings reading the council's methodology and half understanding it, "which means it's a guess with math behind it. A hundred-year flood, they call it, but the hundred years is an average, not a schedule. That part stays uncertain." It was the first time he had said anything like that aloud, the first time he had admitted that a system so precise on the screen could be imprecise about the world, and the admission sat oddly beside the pleasure the maps gave him.

He thought of his father, who had fixed plumbing for thirty years and distrusted anything on a screen that claimed to know a house better than a man standing in its basement. During his last year of school Gabriel had argued with him about exactly this, about some zoning map the city had mailed out, and his father had said that maps were drawn by people who had never gotten wet. Gabriel had been certain, then, that his father was simply behind the times. Now, toggling the layers, he found himself less certain of either position. The map showed Marshview flooded and his father's tools would show Marshview's cracked drainpipes, and neither one, alone, was the whole truth. The counterpoint between them was the point.

A woman came in that afternoon wanting a ferry ticket, and while Gabriel printed it she noticed the screen. She lived in Millbank, she said, high ground, and she wanted to know whether her sister's street in Marshview was in the blue. He showed her. She looked for a long time, then asked whether it meant her sister should sell, and Gabriel, who could have recited the flood probability and the median house age and the parcel values, said that he honestly did not know what it meant for one person's life. The map could say where the water would go. It could not say what her sister owed to a house she'd raised children in.

"She could ask about the buyout program," he offered. "The city has one for the deepest zones." It felt gratuitous to add, a fact offered to fill the silence, and he regretted it even as she wrote the number down, because he was not sure the program had ever actually paid anyone in Marshview, only that it existed somewhere in a PDF he had skimmed.

After she left, he turned the layers off one by one until only the plain street map remained, the kind Mr. Adeyemi sold to tourists, the kind Gabriel had folded and shelved all summer. Then he turned them back on. The blue crept over the eastern districts again, and over it the census blocks, and over everything the small red outlines of houses built before any of this had been mapped, before Tomlinson, before the council's models, before Gabriel. He dragged the cursor across Marshview and watched the parcel numbers flicker under his hand, and printed one of them, and folded the page into his back pocket to show his father.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
The Saturday market smelled of bruised peaches and cut herbs, and Stella moved through it with her grandmother's list folded into her back pocket, though she knew it by heart. Her mother had left that morning for a weekend conference, and the dinner, the first Stella would cook alone for all of them, had landed on her like a prize and like a weight. Her grandmother had made this chicken every Sunday of Stella's childhood, and Stella intended to make it tonight exactly, which was why she stood now in front of the poultry stall, watching a man in a canvas apron wrap two whole birds in butcher paper.

"You want the bigger one," her grandmother used to say, "because a small bird has no generosity in it." Stella had never known whether to ascribe that to experience or to some private doctrine her grandmother had invented and then believed, the way she believed in rinsing everything, twice, under running water. At the stall Stella chose the smaller bird, because there were only four of them now, and carried it in a paper bag against her hip like something newly alive. She caught herself checking the shape of it through the paper, half expecting sentience, half mocking herself for the thought, since a bird this cold and plucked was about as far from a creature as a package of anything.

Her brother Theo was waiting by the tomato crates, eating a sample plum with the guilty speed of someone who intended to take another. He was sixteen and had recently become the kind of person who read pamphlets in waiting rooms and repeated their contents at dinner. "Did you get the bird," he said, not a question, already walking. At home he followed her into the kitchen and leaned on the counter while she unpacked the bag, the peaches, the basil going limp already in their paper, the chicken sweating faintly in its wrapping.

Stella tore the paper away and turned on the faucet and held the bird under it, the way she had watched done a hundred times, cold water running over the pale skin while her grandmother's hands worked the joints and loosened whatever a joint holds. "Stop," Theo said, and he actually stepped forward and turned the faucet off himself, which was a thing he had no right to do and did anyway. "The CDC says not to wash raw chicken. The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the counters, everywhere around it."

"You're being doctrinaire," Stella said, because it was the word that came, and because she wanted a word bigger than his. She was still holding the wet bird over the sink, water dripping off it onto the steel. But Theo only stood there, waiting, and she remembered, unwillingly, a documentary he had made them all watch in March, and she understood that this was not a mood of his, that he had absorbed something and would not unbend from it, and that unbending, in him, was not quite the flaw she wanted it to be.

She set the bird on the cutting board, dry, and dried her own hands, and stood for a moment with her back to him. The problem was not the chicken. The problem was that her grandmother's hands were the first hands she had ever watched cook, and every motion of that cooking was a kind of inheritance, and now some pamphlet-sized fact had walked into the kitchen and told her the inheritance was wrong. She thought about arguing. She thought about saying that her grandmother had fed four generations on washed chicken and every one of them had survived to argue about it. She thought, too, that survival was not the same as proof, and that the arithmetic of germs was invisible and therefore could not be argued with by anecdotes, however beloved.

"It still has to taste like hers," she said finally. "That part isn't negotiable." Theo shrugged and went to wash the tomatoes, then paused, evidently running the same logic through his own doctrine, and wiped them with a damp cloth instead. Stella salted the bird inside and out, more salt than seemed decent, the way her grandmother had, and slid the lemon halves under the skin where they would steam the meat from above and below at once. Some of this, she knew, was gesture, a costume of fidelity. Some of it was real technique, and she could no longer entirely tell which was which, and she decided, for tonight, that she did not have to.

The oven ticked as it heated. Through the window she could see the market tents still up in the distance, white triangles against the hill, and she thought of her grandmother washing that first bird in this same sink, water splashing where Theo's elbows now rested, and she let the two of them sit in her mind together without forcing either one out. The chicken went into the oven at four, and Stella wrote nothing down, and Theo set the table without being asked, putting their mother's place at the head.

"Tell me again why you get the small bird," he said from the doorway.

"Because a big one has no generosity in it," Stella said, and wiped her hands on the towel, and did not tell him whether she believed it.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: Kiddush is a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to begin Sabbath and Jewish festival meals, marking the day as holy.
story:
Lea had said the blessing forty times in the back of her mother's car, and every time, at the same word, her voice thinned and the syllables collapsed into each other. Her grandmother had called on Tuesday and asked, in the tone she used for things already decided, whether Lea would make Kiddush on Friday night, the whole thing, for the whole table. "Your grandfather did it for forty years," her grandmother said. "It's time someone else held the cup."

Lea had said the word Kiddush back to her, uncertainly, and her grandmother had explained only this much: it was the blessing over the wine or grape juice that began Sabbath and festival meals, the words that marked the day as holy. Then she had hung up before Lea could ask why her, or why now, six weeks after the funeral.

Friday afternoon, the house filled the way it always did, which is to say past capacity, cousins orbiting the kitchen, her Uncle David claiming the armchair by the window. Lea carried the silver cup into the pantry to fill it, and found her grandfather's prayer book on the shelf where he had left it, its spine softened by decades of his thumb. The page was worn to a soft gray at exactly the place she needed. She stood among the jars of grape juice her grandmother had bought because Lea didn't drink wine, a courtesy no one had named aloud, and read the Hebrew slowly, her finger under each line, aware that she was doing something circumscribed by rules she only half knew, and that nobody had offered to fill in the other half.

Her little cousin Jonah found her there, drawn by the smell of the braided bread cooling on the counter. "What are you doing hiding," he said, which was not a question. He was nine and treated all rooms as his territory.

"Practicing."

"For what?"

"For tonight." She showed him the cup, which held a dark juice that looked, in that light, almost like the real thing. "There's a blessing that starts the meal. It's called Kiddush. It's over the wine or the juice, and it's what makes the day holy." Saying it to Jonah, she realized, was different from saying it to herself. He was listening the way children listen, with his whole face, and the words had to stand up straight.

"Can I hear it?"

"No," she said, and then, because his face began to fall, "It's not ready. If I practice it in front of you it'll use it up."

He accepted this, the way children accept all false economies, and went to find the bread.

At the table, her grandmother's good cloth was laid, and the candles had already been blessed by her mother, their light making the crowded room gentler than it was. Everyone found seats, and the noise lowered itself without being told to. Her grandmother poured the grape juice into the silver cup until it rose past the middle, which someone had once told Lea was required, though she no longer remembered who, and set it in front of her with both hands.

The room was quiet in the way rooms are quiet when they are waiting, and Lea understood that the silence was not duress, whatever it felt like. It was an invitation shaped like a test. She lifted the cup, and the weight of it surprised her, more than she had expected from practicing with a water glass in the car.

She began. The words she had drilled came out, and the word that always failed her did not fail her, and she could hear, in the strange acoustics of a full dining room, her own voice doing something it had never done in the back seat of the car. She was aware of her grandfather's absence as a shape in the room, an empty chair that was not empty tonight because Uncle David had been moved into it, and she held both of those facts together: that he was gone, and that the blessing did not stop being his, exactly, even as it passed through her. She did not know yet what she believed about any of it, the holiness, the day marked off from other days, and she let the not-knowing sit beside the words without pushing either one away.

When she finished, she drank, and the juice was sweeter than she had expected, and she passed the cup to her grandmother, who drank and passed it on. It went around the table hand to hand, cup after cup poured, everyone drinking, even Jonah, who made a face at the sweetness and then drank again. The meal began the way meals begin, in noise and the passing of plates, and nothing in the room announced that anything had changed, and yet something evanescent had happened and hung there anyway, refusing to be nothing.

After the soup, her grandmother leaned over and straightened the prayer book beside Lea's plate, which had slid crooked, and left her hand on it a moment. "Same time next month," she said. "You'll do the bread blessing too."

Lea looked at the book, at her grandmother's hand, at the candles burning low in their holders. "Teach me tomorrow," she said. "Before everyone leaves."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
Maxime arrived at the pool at six forty, before the lifeguards had finished unhooking the lane ropes, because Coach Reyes had told him that if he wanted to write his own training program he would have to see the pool empty first. He had a spiral notebook and a pencil he kept behind his ear like a carpenter. On the whiteboard by the office, someone had written lap swim 7-9 in blue marker, and beneath it, in different handwriting, GO MAXIME, which he suspected was his little sister, Noor, who had a key because she fed the filter fish in the office tank.

He wanted this program more than he had wanted anything since he'd made the county squad at fifteen. Two weeks ago he'd watched regionals from the bleachers, third alternate, and his father had put a hand on his shoulder and said nothing, which in their family's patrimony of silence was roughly a eulogy. So Maxime had drawn a grid on the first page of the notebook, seven columns, and filled Monday through Sunday with drills, kick sets, sprints, more drills, until his friend Dana had looked at it over lunch and gone morose in the particular way she did when she thought someone was about to ruin themselves.

"Where's the rest," she said.

"Rest is for people who aren't behind," Maxime said, and she had rolled her eyes so hard she had to steady her sandwich.

That had been Thursday. Now it was Saturday morning, and Noor was sitting cross-legged on the diving block with a book about sleep, of all things, because she was doing a school project on it and had sequestered herself at the pool where, she claimed, the hum of the pumps helped her think. She read aloud without being asked, which was her way of being useful. "In a 2011 Stanford study," she read, "basketball players who aimed for ten hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from seven point nine to eight point eight successful shots out of ten."

"That can't be right," Maxime said, treading water at the end of lane four. "Ten hours? Who has ten hours?"

"They aimed for it," Noor said. "In bed. Nightly." She turned the page as though the matter were settled.

He pulled himself out and sat dripping on the gutter, doing the arithmetic he could not stop doing lately. He practiced four hours a day. He also stayed up until two most nights, doing homework badly, watching videos of the Beijing final frame by frame, lying in the dark composing programs in his head. If the basketball players had gone from 7.9 to 8.8 out of ten just from being in bed, then the hours he spent planning at 2 a.m. were not hours in the bank. They were withdrawals. He wrote in the notebook, in the Saturday column where he had scheduled a fourth sprint set, the word SLEEP, then crossed it out because it looked stupid, then wrote it again smaller.

Dana arrived at nine with a thermos and her own agenda, which she announced immediately. "I need the shallow lane at four for the kids' lesson," she said. She had been trying for a month to get the rec department to let her run a beginners' class for the neighborhood kids, some of whom, she said, only knew how to jump in and hold their breath. "If you're writing the big fancy program, put it in the program. You have the coach's ear. I don't."

"I have the coach's elbow," Maxime said. "She gives me the whiteboard sometimes."

"Then write it on the whiteboard and photograph it. Guilt is a renewable resource."

He laughed, and then, because he was thinking about the grid, he pulled Dana down to sit on the wet concrete and showed her the page. "Tell me what's wrong with it," he said, "but the real thing, not the rest thing."

She looked at it for a long time, chewing the thermos cap. "There's no warm-up that isn't just swimming slower," she said finally. "You go from nothing to fifty-meter repeats like the water owes you money. And Saturday is insane, and Sunday is insane, and everything's insane. But the warm-up thing, that's the structural one."

He thought about the basketball players again, their free throws rising by almost a whole shot out of ten, and about how he had always believed the body was a machine you ran hotter and hotter. The study said nothing about why, and Noor's book said nothing more, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he did not know whether ten hours of bed would do anything at all for a swimmer, or whether it only worked on shooters, or whether it was one of those findings that evaporated when you tried to live inside it. But there was a version of his program where the drills were the same and the container around them was different, and he could not find a reason not to test it except vanity, which he did not think was a reason.

He erased the week with the side of his fist, which smeared, and started over. Monday, drills, after a real warm-up, ankle rotations and band work and eight easy laps. Wednesday, drills. Friday, drills, shorter. Sunday, nothing. In the margin he wrote 10 hrs in bed? with the question mark, because he refused to write it as a command when he did not yet believe it as one. Then, because Dana was still waiting, he took the blue marker and wrote beneath lap swim: 4 PM SHALLOW LANE, DANA'S KIDS' CLASS, and drew a sun around it so the lifeguards could not miss it.

"You didn't have to do the sun," Dana said, but she was smiling into her thermos.

At four o'clock he came back to watch, ostensibly to time his own easy laps, actually to see whether anyone showed up. Six kids came, two of them the twins from building C who had never been in water deeper than their bathtub, and Dana got in first and held out both hands, and the smaller twin took them and stepped off the edge into the shallow lane with her whole face scrunched like a person leaping off a cliff.

"Kick," Dana said. "Like you're mad at the water."

The kid kicked, and moved, and came up spitting and delighted, and Maxime wrote one more line in the notebook, and it said only: water temp 26, she'll need the shorter noodles.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
Dominic had the kitchen to himself by four o'clock, which was the only reason he had agreed to do it. His mother was on her second shift at the clinic, his father had taken the twins to a birthday party, and his grandmother was in the living room with the television turned to a panel show where one pundit after another explained the economy to nobody in particular. He had promised a proper dinner, not pasta from a box, and he had decided on breaded chicken with a homemade aioli, because a kid at school had brought some in a jar once and Dominic had thought about it for a week.

The recipe said to whisk one egg yolk with mustard and lemon, then add a cup of oil in a thin stream while whisking without stopping. He set the bowl on a damp towel so it would not skate across the counter, separated the yolk with the shells the way his grandmother had shown him years ago, and began. For a while it worked. The mixture turned pale and thick and he felt the particular smugness of someone watching a plan hold together. Then his elbow knocked the measuring cup and a quarter cup of oil went in at once, and the whole thing went thin and strange, oil floating in a yellowish liquid that refused to combine no matter how hard he whipped it.

He stood over the bowl, whisk in hand, doing the arithmetic of the evening. If the sauce was ruined he would fall back on butter, which was fine, which was what everyone expected anyway. He was still deciding when his grandmother came in for water and stopped beside him. She looked at the bowl and then at him. "Split," she said. He said yes, he had ruined it, he was sorry. She pulled a chair from the table and sat down.

"You started with the yolk?" she asked. He said he had, one yolk, exactly like the recipe. "And it broke when the oil came in too fast." She reached into the fridge, took out another egg, and handed it to him without standing up. "Clean bowl. Yolk in it, a spoon of the broken mess, whisk. Then the rest of the oil, slow." He asked what the second yolk could possibly do that the first one had not done, and she said, "Lecithin," as if that settled it. When he kept whisking without understanding, she added that the proteins in the yolk were emulsifiers too, and that was what held the oil in the water, tiny drops, kept apart so the sauce did not come apart.

He cracked the egg, dropped in a spoon of the curdled mixture, and whisked. It thickened almost immediately, faster than the first batch had, and he added the oil a few milliliters at a time, his wrist aching, watching the sauce climb the wires of the whisk in a slow gleam that seemed to burnish the steel itself. When it held, he stood back and looked at it. His grandmother drank her water and said it was the same with people, and he said probably, and she laughed at him for that.

While the chicken rested under foil, she stayed in the chair and grew querulous about the panel show, the pundits, the state of everything, and he listened with half his attention because the other half was still on the bowl. He had started the evening believing that a recipe was a set of instructions you followed and it worked or it didn't, and that his failure meant the dinner was over. Now he understood that the sauce had not failed so much as run out of its capacity, and that capacity could be added back in, one yolk at a time. But he was honest enough with himself to notice what he did not know: he could not have predicted the split, and he could not have said how much oil one yolk could hold before the next failure, and if his grandmother had not come in for water he would be melting butter.

The twins came home loud, his father behind them with cake, and they ate at the table with the aioli in a dish in the center, everyone dipping, nobody asking where it came from. His father said it was better than the store kind, and Dominic said he had almost thrown it out, and told the story of the second yolk. The twins wanted to know if they could break one on purpose next time and fix it, and he said he didn't see why not, though he wasn't sure they'd learn anything that way, since fixing a thing you'd broken on purpose was different from fixing a thing you needed.

Later, washing the dishes while his grandmother dried, he thought about telling her he had decided something, that he understood things now, and he decided against saying it out loud because it wasn't entirely true. He knew what he had seen. He knew the rescue worked. Whether the whole evening had been a success or a near miss depended on a question he couldn't answer, which was how much of the result was him and how much was the egg. His grandmother put the last bowl in the cabinet and turned off the light over the stove.

"Next time," she said, "use a bigger bowl."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Hindu festival of Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and begins with a bonfire the night before called Holika Dahan.
story:
The bonfire was taller than Jeremy's uncle's house, which meant it was tall enough that the fire marshal, if such a person existed in this part of town, would have wept. Jeremy stood at the edge of the temple parking lot with his cousin Priya, who was explaining, with much gesticulating, exactly how the thing was going to collapse.

"It always leans north," she said, flapping her arm like a heron. "Every year. And every year my dad says it won't, and every year it does, and every year we move the aunties."

Jeremy had come because his mother had come, and because missing Holi at his aunt's temple was not an option that anyone had offered him. It was the night before the colors, the night of the fire itself, and the parking lot smelled like diesel and marigolds, which he decided was not a bad smell, just an honest one.

"I looked it up," he said. "The whole thing is astronomical. It's the full moon of Phalguna, usually in March. The fire's tonight, and the colors tomorrow morning, because the festival starts with the bonfire the night before."

Priya squinted at him. "Did you just learn my own religion off the internet?"

"Parts of it. I wanted to know why the date moves around."

"And what did the internet say about why the fire leans north?"

"That wasn't covered."

Her father overheard them, because her father overheard everything, and he arrived in the phlegmatic way he had, moving as though the crowd parted around him by prior arrangement. "It's called Holika Dahan," he said, and patted the woodpile like a horse he had trained. Then he went back to arguing with three men about the lean, which, Jeremy noted, leaned north.

Priya tugged Jeremy's sleeve. "Come on. If you're going to be an investigator, investigate."

She led him past the aunties on their folding chairs, past a boy trying to trade a laddu for a sparkler, to the temple's back hallway, where a bulletin board held a printout of the festival schedule. It was there, under a heading in both English and Hindi: Holika Dahan, full moon night, Phalguna. March, this year. Below it, a paragraph about Prahlad and the demon Holika, who could not be burned and who burned anyway, because protection, the paragraph said, does not belong to the one who misuses it.

"So it's a story about a fire that didn't do what it was supposed to," Jeremy said.

"It's a story about a fire that did what it was supposed to. You have it backwards."

"Fine. It's a story where the fire had a moral."

"That's not so strange. Your chemistry teacher has opinions about sodium."

He laughed, and then he didn't, because something in it snagged. He had spent the drive over rehearsing what he'd say if anyone asked, some version of I'm here for family, not for the metaphysics, which was a sentence he'd invented in the car and already regretted. But standing in the hallway with the schedule, he found he couldn't keep the two things apart so cleanly. The date was the full moon, that was physics. The fire was Holika, that was story. And the wood was leaning north, and the crowd was singing, and the whole thing was one event, not two, whatever he'd planned to say about it.

Outside, the singing had gotten louder. Priya grabbed his wrist. "It's starting. Watch the lean. Watch it."

The priest circled the pile with a lamp, and the men with the long poles set the base alight, and the flames took their time, the way big fires do, and then found the diesel and stopped taking their time. The heat arrived before the sound of the crowd. And the pile leaned. It leaned north, majestically, in flagrant disregard of her father's predictions, and a hundred phones went up, and somebody's uncle began gesticulating at the structure as though he could negotiate with it.

"North," Priya shouted over the roar. "Say it."

"North. I concede everything."

Her father appeared behind them, arms crossed, watching the pillar of sparks climb toward a sky where, if the smoke hadn't been in the way, the full moon would have been sitting right there, exactly on schedule, in its month, doing its ancient work. "The lean is traditional," he announced, without a hint of apology, and Priya made a noise like a kettle.

"Tomorrow," she told Jeremy, "you get the colors. Fair warning, I have three buckets and no mercy, and I know you didn't bring a white shirt on purpose."

"I didn't bring a white shirt because I'm not a fool."

"You'll stand out anyway," she said, and shoved a laddu into his hand, and pulled him back toward the fire before the aunties claimed all the good folding chairs.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word valedictorian comes from the Latin vale dicere, meaning "to say farewell," which is why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech.
story:
The folding chair had her name on it, a strip of masking tape with CLAIRE V. in her principal's hurried print, and she sat down in the empty row of chairs an hour before anyone else would arrive. In her lap sat nine index cards, covered and recovered in her slanted handwriting, and the problem had not shrunk overnight. She could talk about resilience. She could talk about the future. Both options made her stomach turn, not because they were wrong but because they were borrowed, phrases worn smooth by every graduating class since the invention of folding chairs.

"Yo u up?" read the text from Dee, which was Dee's way of spelling "You're early." Claire texted back a photo of the chairs, the taped name, the white riser where the podium stood. "Coming," Dee wrote. "Don't abscond with my speech."

Dee was the salutatorian, a fact she had stopped pretending not to mind around March, when the final GPA had come down to a tenth of a point. She crossed the field now in the flat gray dress she'd argued about with her mother, carrying two coffees and her own cards, fewer than Claire's, held together with a rubber band. Her want was simple and she'd stated it plainly at lunch last week: she wanted to be funny. She'd spent three years being the smart one, the one teachers called on when no one else raised a hand, and she wanted, once, to make a whole stadium laugh on purpose.

"Read me the opening," Dee said, dropping into the chair beside her. Claire read it. Something about journeys and thresholds. Dee drank her coffee and said nothing, which in Dee's language was a verdict.

"I keep trying to write the ending," Claire said. "The goodbye part. And everything I write sounds like a greeting card ate a thesaurus. Like I'm performing erudition I don't actually have."

"So look it up. That's what you do." Dee tipped her chin at Claire's phone. "You're the one who found out the mascot was designed by a junior in 1974."

Claire already had the dictionary app open; that was the truth of it, she'd been typing before Dee finished the sentence. Valedictorian. She scrolled past the pronunciation, past the definition she knew, and found the etymology line near the bottom, small gray text under the entry.

"It comes from vale dicere," she read aloud. "Latin. It means 'to say farewell.' That's why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech. It's the whole job. I've been trying to write a speech about the future when the word itself is just asking me to say goodbye."

"Huh," Dee said, and stole one of Claire's index cards to write it down,vale dicere,in her rounder handwriting, and beneath it: "so it's not about being smart?"

The question sat between them longer than a question that size should. Because Claire had spent four years treating the title as a verdict, a number that proved something, and here was the word confessing that it had never been about that at all. It was about the leaving. The person with the highest grades had been assigned, by language itself, the task of standing up in front of everyone and admitting that this was over. She wasn't sure yet whether that was a relief or a heavier thing.

"So write the goodbye," Dee said. "Say what you'd actually miss. Not the building. Not the, like, hallowed halls."

"Marcus folding cheese pizza in half like a sandwich."

"The smell of the biology wing after the fetal pig unit."

They went on like that, trading specifics, and Claire wrote fast, filling a fresh card, then another. Somewhere in the middle of it she noticed the incipient ceremony assembling around them: a man on a ladder straightening the banner, the band hauling percussion up the riser steps, her grandmother's Buick pulling into the far lot, early the way her grandmother was early for everything, a woman who considered timeliness a form of love. Claire felt the strangest double pull, wanting the morning to stretch and wanting it over, and could not have said which wanting was stronger.

"Your turn to rehearse," she told Dee. "Show me funny."

Dee stood, cleared her throat at the empty stadium as if it were full, and delivered her opening line about the tenth of a point, a joke about how she'd asked the guidance office whether she could appeal it using attendance. The joke needed work. The delivery needed more work. But Dee grinned the whole way through, and somewhere out past center field a crow lifted off the goalpost and beat away over the treeline.

Claire looked down at her cards, the Latin copied twice in two hands. She still didn't know how to end the speech. She knew only that she would stand at that podium this afternoon and say farewell, in whatever clumsy words arrived, and that maybe the clumsiness was the point. She turned the taped chair around so the name faced her and said, quietly, "Vale."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
story:
The parking lot behind the closed hardware store had faded lines and one leaning light pole, and Savannah had chosen it because her mother would never think to look for her here. She sat in the driver's seat of the borrowed Corolla with her hands at ten and two, the way the pamphlet showed, while Mr. Okafor settled into the passenger seat and dropped a clipboard on his knee.

"I'm going to get my license before Labor Day," she said. "I have to. My brother's in a rehab place forty minutes out, and my mother works, and the visitation hours are two to four on Sundays." She had rehearsed the whole speech in the shower, and now it came out too fast, like she was afraid he would stop her.

Mr. Okafor buckled his seatbelt. "Turn the engine on first. Then we can litigate your Sunday plans."

She turned the key. The car shuddered awake under her, and she gripped the wheel harder than she needed to. For twenty minutes they did nothing but circles, wide lazy arcs around the light pole, her foot learning the small difference between the brake and the almost-brake. Twice she killed the engine and twice she restarted it without being told, and Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard both times, which she decided not to ask about.

"All right," he said finally. "Parking lot's done. We go on the road."

The road was a two-lane stretch behind the strip mall, empty enough at nine in the morning that she could hear her own pulse. She merged, sort of, and drove, and it was working, it was actually working, until she came up behind a delivery truck and realized she was close enough to read the phone number printed on its back doors. Her mother, who read contracts for a living and had once called Savannah's driving school contract "trenchant, in the way a dull knife is trenchant," would have said she was drafting a subpoena for a collision. Savannah eased off the gas but drifted forward again anyway, her foot convinced that closer meant safer, that if she could see the truck's mirrors the truck could see her.

"Don't slow down," Mr. Okafor said. "Just do something else. Watch the truck ahead of us. When it passes a fixed point, like that lamppost coming up, count seconds until we reach that same point."

"Why?"

"Try it. Out loud."

The truck's back bumper crossed the base of the lamppost. "One one-thousand, two one-thousand," she said, and her front bumper arrived at the same lamppost just after two. She checked the mirror. The gap between her and the truck looked enormous now, a whole polite room of empty pavement, and nothing bad had happened because of it. The truck hadn't escaped her. Nobody had honked. She tried it again at the next signpost, watching the truck pass the sign and counting, and got to three one-thousand before she reached it, and it still felt wrong, still felt like she was letting the world get ahead of her, but the wrongness was only in her foot, which kept wanting to close the gap like an apology.

"It's called the two-second rule," Mr. Okafor said, "in case anybody asks."

They drove to the end of the strip and back. Savannah held her count the whole way, at signs and mailboxes and a fire hydrant with a dented cap, and at a red light she sat with her hands still at ten and two and thought about her mother, who had spent the whole summer after Danny's arrest saying that if you loved people you stayed close to them, you stayed on their case, you did not let one inch open up between you. Savannah had believed her, had practically moved into Danny's room. But Danny had told her, the last visit, through plexiglass, that the inch was the only place he could breathe. She looked at the gap between her car and the truck idling ahead, counted it out of habit, three seconds, plenty, and thought that maybe you could hold on to people and still leave them room to move, though she couldn't have said where the holding stopped and the room began. That part she would have to work out the way she was working out the brake, by doing it and getting it wrong and doing it again.

"Same time Thursday," Mr. Okafor said when she parked, crooked but within the lines. "You'll count your way onto the highway."

"Thursday," she said. She was already planning the route to Danny's, every sign and lamppost along it, counting the seconds between her and everything ahead.

fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
story:
Logan's father backed the sedan into the far corner of the Kmart lot, where the painted lines had faded to the color of old bone, and cut the engine. "Switch," he said, and got out into the November wind without another word, which was his way of pretending this was ordinary.

It was not ordinary. Logan had waited since August, when his mother had taken him to the licensing office for the permit test and then, at the last minute, refused to come inside. She sat in the car with the heater running while he stood in line beneath a poster he read four times because the line barely moved. The poster said that according to the CDC, drivers aged sixteen to nineteen had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven. He had passed the test, walked out with the paper card in his fist, and slid into the passenger seat without mentioning the poster, and his mother had driven home on the far right of the road, both hands on the wheel, and said nothing either.

Now, four months later, his father tossed the keys across the roof of the car and Logan caught them against his chest. He adjusted the mirror too far, corrected it, adjusted it again. His father had already lowered the radio, which had been droning about inflation and stalled growth and something the commentator called stagflation, a word Logan filed away to look up later, though he gathered from context it meant prices climbing while the economy went nowhere, a kind of trap with no exit.

"Feet first," his father said. "Brake, then start it." Logan pressed the brake and the engine turned over and the whole car hummed around him like something alive that had merely been sleeping. He let off the brake too soon and they rolled an inch before he clamped down, and his father laughed, one short syllable, not unkind.

For half an hour it was only this: gas, brake, the wheel pulled in slow ovals around the empty cart corrals. Logan discovered that the car was parsimonious with information, telling him almost nothing until he asked with his hands and feet, and then telling him everything at once. His father said "wider" and "earlier" and once, quietly, "you're begging the wheel, don't beg it," and Logan understood that the machine could not be coaxed or beguiled into gentleness. It did exactly what he did, only larger.

"Pull up to that light pole and stop," his father said. "Then back around it." Logan lined up on the pole, checked the mirror his mother would have checked, and eased backward, and it was there, in the crooked slow arc of reverse, that the poster came back to him whole. Almost three times, per mile driven. He let the car stop and sat with his hands at ten and two.

"Dad," he said. "Did Mom see that poster at the DMV? The one about teen drivers." His father was quiet long enough that the ticking of the cooling engine became audible. "She stood outside last time because of it," he finally said. "August. You were inside taking the test and she was reading it through the window. She made me promise not to tell you."

Logan looked out at the empty lot, the cart corral, the light pole he had just circled without hitting. He thought of her silence on the drive home and had read it, all these months, as disappointment in him, and now he could not tell whether it had been fear instead, or whether the two were even separable. The numbers were the numbers. He was sixteen, and per mile he was more dangerous than his father, and no amount of care in this lot changed that yet; and still his mother had signed the permission slip, and still his father had driven him here, and both of those were also facts. "So she's been scared this whole time," Logan said, and it was not quite a question.

"She's been letting you drive anyway," his father said. "Same thing, sometimes." He pointed at the far end of the lot, where the empty spaces stretched out in long faded rows. "Take us down there. Full stop at the last line, and then home."

Logan checked the mirror, signaled out of habit into the emptiness, and pressed the gas.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
Henry got the job the first week of June, which felt like a small miracle because he had assumed, all spring, that nobody would hire a sixteen-year-old who had never held anything resembling a position. The aquatic center hired him anyway, handed him a red whistle and a shirt two sizes too large, and put him in the tall chair by the deep end. He learned to watch the water the way his instructor had described it, in layers: the surface, where nothing was usually wrong, and beneath it, where everything could be.

By the middle of July he had stopped being nervous. He could spot an incipient panic from thirty feet away, a child whose strokes shortened and whose head bobbed a beat too fast, and he would slide down the ladder before the panic had a name. His mother said the job suited him. His father, who worked double shifts at the plant and considered rest a foreign country, said only, "Pick up hours when they offer them. You won't be sixteen forever."

So when the assistant manager, Dara, asked who could cover shifts during the county swim meet weekend, Henry raised his hand. He covered Marcus on Friday, covered two split shifts on Saturday, and came in Sunday for a birthday party of eleven eight-year-olds whose parents seemed to regard the lifeguard as a kind of rented conscience. By Sunday night his shoulders were sunburned and his legs ached from the ladder, and when he clocked out he counted the hours in his head and got forty-nine.

The paycheck came two Thursdays later. He read it standing at the mailbox in the wet heat, and the number was wrong, or rather it was wrong in a way that made it more right than he expected. The last several hours were paid at a higher rate than the rest, one and a half times what he usually made, as near as he could figure. He did the arithmetic twice on the back of a pool schedule he'd shoved in his back pocket. It checked out.

At work the next morning he found Dara at the front desk, sorting keys.

"Some of my hours were paid at a higher rate," he said. "Is that right?"

"Overtime," Dara said, not looking up. "Hours beyond forty in a workweek. One and a half times your regular rate. It's federal law for employees like us." She fished out a key, handed it to a man in a damp towel, and turned back. "Why, you didn't know?"

He hadn't. He had assumed that extra shifts meant extra money in a straight line, hour stacked on hour, and it had honestly never occurred to him that the law bent the line after forty. He felt something between gratitude and unease, the way he sometimes felt when a rule protected him for reasons he hadn't earned.

That afternoon, sitting in the tall chair, he thought about his father. His father spoke about the plant the way some people speak about the weather, as a thing that happened to him. Henry had heard him vilify management at dinner, then take a double the next day, and he had never understood how both could be true at once. Now he thought he saw it a little: his father worked the doubles because the money after forty was better money, and he resented that the better money existed only because the first forty had wrung him out. It was not hypocrisy. It was arithmetic with a wound in it.

Marcus climbed the ladder to relieve him at four. Marcus was nineteen, tanned, and indifferent to nearly everything except his car.

"You picked up the whole meet weekend," Marcus said, settling into the chair. "That's like a religious commitment. Lifeguard asceticism."

"It was forty-nine hours," Henry said.

"Saint Henry of the Deep End." Marcus blew the whistle at a kid running near the gutter, a short corrective blast. "I'd never do it. I did it one summer and stopped seeing my friends entirely. Money's money, but."

He said it lightly, the way people say things they mean more than they want to show. Henry looked at the water, which was calm, all layers of it, and considered that he had spent a weekend he would otherwise have spent with Eli and Sam at the creek, and that the check in his pocket had a number in it he liked, and that he could not yet tell which of those mattered more. He suspected the answer would change, and he suspected he would not always get to choose when.

Dara caught him at the gate as he left. "We need coverage again next weekend," she said. "Friday through Sunday. There's a meet."

Henry stood with his hand on the chain link, the whistle still warm in his pocket.

"Can I take just Friday?" he said. "Just the one day?"

Dara shrugged and wrote it on the clipboard. Behind her, the pool lay flat and bright, and a kid on the diving board was counting his toes in preparation for something reckless.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
The decision was supposed to post at five o'clock, which meant Abigail spent seventh period in Mr. Okafor's Human Geography class with her phone face-down in her backpack and her heart rate somewhere near the ceiling. The room smelled like dry-erase marker and the oranges Marcus peeled every day without fail, dropping the rind in a slow pile beside his map of Central Asia. Mr. Okafor was drawing the Eurasian steppe on the board, a long flat grassland he shaded in green, and Abigail copied it into her notes without processing a single word.

Marcus leaned over during the worksheet. "You're writing steppe on top of Poland," he said.

"Am I."

"You've written it four times. Abigail."

She looked down. Four steppes, stacked like sedimentary layers across Eastern Europe, each one slightly crooked. She crossed them out. At five o'clock the portal would either show a word like congratulations or a word like regret, and everything she'd done for four years had already been boiled down to whichever one appeared, and no amount of knowing that was unreasonable made it stop being true.

"Hey," Marcus said, quieter. "Remember March."

"March," she said.

"When you took the SAT. You came out of that room looking like you'd seen a ghost. You told me the second math module was brutal."

She remembered it exactly. The testing room had been cold enough that her fingers slipped on the trackpad, and when the harder questions started stacking up, question after question she couldn't immediately untangle, she had been certain she was failing. She'd ridden home on the bus constructing an apology to her parents.

"And then I told you," Marcus said. "It's adaptive now. Since March of 2024, the SAT in the U.S. is digital, and it adapts. How you do on the first module of each section sets how hard the second module is. So if the second one felt impossible, that probably meant you'd earned the hard one. You did well enough on the first module that the test gave you the tough second." He tapped her worksheet. "And then your score came back and you screamed in the cafeteria and made a senior drop his pizza."

"I didn't make him drop it."

"You made him drop it."

She had gotten a 780 in math, a number no one could impugn, and she had felt, for about a week, like a person the world made sense to. Then she'd written her essays and hit submit and gone back to being a person checking her email eleven times a day. The adaptive test had at least been legible. Work hard on module one, receive module two, read the difficulty of your own future off the difficulty of your questions. Colleges were not adaptive. Colleges made you wait five weeks and then posted all decisions at the same hour on the same Friday, and gave you no module two at all.

The clock said 2:47. Mr. Okafor moved on to rain shadow deserts. Marcus went back to his worksheet, and the oranges sat in their rind pile, and someone's pencil case zipper went up and down three times in the back row.

At 3:31, in study hall, her phone buzzed once, face-up this time because she'd given up on dignity. An email from the admissions office. Not the decision, she realized after her stomach had already dropped; a notice that decisions would post at 5:00 as planned, with a link to the portal and a sentence thanking applicants for their patience. Abigail laughed out loud, alone at a library table, a short ugly bark that made the boy across from her look up from his flashcards.

At 5:04 she was home, on the floor of her room with the laptop actually on her lap, because sitting in a chair felt too casual for the occasion. The portal took forty seconds to load. The screen was pale and the fan hummed against her knees the whole time.

The word was "deferred." Not congratulations, not regret. We have not yet reached a final decision on your application, the letter said, and we will revisit it in the spring.

She sat there while the fan hummed. She had done well on the first module, she thought, and she had done well on the second, and the test had told her so with numbers, and this told her nothing except wait. There was no reading the difficulty of this off anything. Marcus texted a picture of the steppe worksheet with the word LOL under her four crooked crossings-out.

She typed back, "deferred," and then, before she could decide whether it was a joke, "the questions got harder. so I must be doing great."

From downstairs her mother called that dinner was in ten minutes. Abigail closed the laptop, and the room went quiet except for the fan winding down.
