fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
I had always been careful with lists, and this one was no exception: eleven colleges, ranked, with columns for average aid, distance from home, and whether they had a real Classics department, because I had decided, sometime in October, that I was going to be a polymath, a person who read Latin and coded in Python and could not be reduced to a single line on a resume. My brother Theo said that was just a fancy word for being unable to choose, but Theo was thirteen and believed this was a character flaw.

I sat at the kitchen computer because my laptop had died in November, and because the kitchen was where my mother was, wrapping candle orders for her holiday rush. The Common App glowed in front of me, seven of eleven applications done, and I told myself I did not care about the money part, which was, I understand now, the first thing I got wrong. I believed I had arranged everything so that finances were not the deciding factor. I had even told my college counselor, Ms. Okafor, that I refused to let money pick my school, as though refusing to look at something made it disappear.

"Which ones are left?" my mother asked, not looking up from her tissue paper.

"Carver, Halstead, Ryland, and Dupre," I said. "The good ones."

"The expensive ones," she said, mild, and I said, "Aid exists, Mom," in the voice I used when I wanted a subject closed. She let it close. That was her way; she noticed when I was gripping the mouse too hard and simply set a mug of tea at my elbow without comment.

Carver I submitted in ten minutes, my essay about translating Catullus at the laundromat already uploaded. Halstead took longer because Halstead wanted an extra paragraph on "intellectual curiosity," a phrase I found nearly meaningless. It was while fact-checking a statistic about Halstead's Classics department that I found the thread that unraveled everything: a forum post from a student saying that at some schools, applying for financial aid actually affected your chances of admission. I had assumed the opposite, obviously, because it would be monstrous otherwise, because money should not get to vote on your worth.

I clicked through to a table on a college data site and cross-checked it twice. Some colleges were need-blind, meaning they decided whom to admit without ever considering whether the applicant could afford to pay. Many others, and this was the part that made my ears go hot, were need-aware instead, which meant they did look. I checked the table against my list. Ryland and Dupre, my two remaining reaches, the ones I had been calling my dreams since September, were need-aware. Halstead, which I had just submitted with a financial aid application attached, was need-aware too.

"Mom," I said. "Do you know what need-blind means?"

She came over, hands still dusty with tissue paper, and read the screen. "No," she said. "Tell me."

"It means they admit you without looking at whether you can pay. Some schools do that. A lot of them don't." Saying it out loud, I heard how naive my earlier confidence had been, all that October certainty about not letting money decide, as if I had been the one in control. I had built my list on prestige and Latin and weather, and had never once checked this column, because checking it felt like admitting what we were, and I did not want our finances to be something that could stigmatize me even on paper. That was the second thing I got wrong, and it was worse than the first.

Theo wandered in, saw my face, and asked if somebody died. "Nobody died," I said. "I have to redo my list." And that, in the end, was what I did, though redoing is too tidy a word for it. I spent two hours at the kitchen table with the table printed out, my mother drying mugs beside me, moving Ryland and Dupre from the dream column to the honest column, where they stayed, because being need-aware did not make them villains and did not make me a charity case; it made them a risk I could see instead of one I couldn't. I added three need-blind schools I had dismissed as boring, and one of them, it turned out, had a scholar program for exactly the kind of unfocused, voracious reader I actually was, the kind Theo mocked. The worry that students like me, patching together aid, were somehow an underclass at the fancy schools, that this anxiety was endemic rather than particular to me, was a worry I could name now but not settle. I would not know until March whether any of it mattered.

At eleven, my mother went to bed and Theo left his half-finished algebra homework on the counter, a small surrender. I reopened the Common App, read my Catullus essay once more, and pressed submit on the first of the need-blind schools, then sat listening to the modem-shaped silence that follows.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Compound interest follows A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where n is how many times per year interest is added, so more frequent compounding gives a slightly larger total.
story:
The drive down from Silverton took an hour and a half, long enough for the last of her battery to bleed out somewhere past the reservoir, so Vanessa walked into the phone store holding a dead black rectangle instead of a phone. The town where she lived was small and montane, a shelf of houses pinned between two ridgelines, and the nearest store that sold anything was down here in the valley, in a strip mall between a nail salon and a credit union. Her phone was four years old. The battery had been dying by noon since spring, and yesterday it had shut itself off during her college interview, mid-sentence, while a woman on a screen in Denver waited for her to finish an answer about the book that had changed her life.

She had two hundred and twelve dollars, most of it from a summer bussing tables, sitting in an account at that credit union her grandmother had opened when Vanessa turned fifteen. The phone she wanted, the one with the camera good enough for the photography elective she'd been admitted to, cost seven hundred ninety-nine. A clerk named Deshawn, who kept a desiccated little cactus on the counter behind the register and clearly hadn't watered it in a year, slid a glossy card across the glass. Financing, he said. No money down, twenty-four payments, and she could walk out with the phone today. He smiled when he said today, the way people smile when they're handing you something.

Vanessa asked what the payments were. He turned the card over and pointed at a table of numbers, small ones at first, and she did what she did in math class, which was multiply. Twenty-four of this, plus an origination fee, plus a rate that got added because she was seventeen and had never borrowed anything and would need her mother to co-sign. The total came out to more than seven hundred ninety-nine. Not catastrophically more, but more, and when she asked why, Deshawn said, "That's the interest. That's how lending works. You're paying for the use of their money over time." He said it kindly, without any speech attached, and turned to help a man in a Carhartt jacket who was tapping a display phone with one finger like it might be fake.

While she waited she drifted next door, partly for something to do and partly because the credit union had a rack of pamphlets by the door and she was seventeen with two hundred and twelve dollars and a phone problem, which is to say she was in the mood to look at anything with numbers on it. A brochure about savings accounts for members under eighteen showed two options side by side. Both paid three percent. One compounded monthly, one yearly, and at the bottom, in faint gray print the size of ants, was the formula: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). Under it, a note the designer had probably been told to include and had done so as unobtrusively as possible: n is the number of times per year interest is added.

She borrowed a pen from the counter. She had no calculator, because her calculator was a dead phone, so she worked it out longhand on the back of a deposit slip, slowly, checking herself. Five hundred dollars, three percent, one year, annual compounding: five hundred times one point zero three, five hundred fifteen. Then the monthly one. Three percent divided by twelve, that tiny fraction, raised to the twelfth power. She multiplied it out digit by digit, and the answer was five hundred fifteen dollars and a bit of change. More than the other one. Not by much, a dollar and change on five hundred, but more, and the difference came from nothing except how often they added the interest. She sat with that for a second. The same rate, the same year, and the money that got touched twelve times came out slightly ahead.

So here was what she knew, standing between the two buildings. If she borrowed, seven hundred ninety-nine would quietly become more than seven hundred ninety-nine, the way water runs downhill, without her ever feeling it leave. If she saved, two hundred and twelve would become slightly more than two hundred and twelve, the way a plant grows, also without her feeling it. The two facts faced each other in her head like people on opposite benches, and she couldn't make them shake hands. One said walk out with the phone today. The other said the future version of her, the one in college, would be either slightly richer or slightly poorer depending on this afternoon, and that version of her was the one who needed the camera.

She went back into the phone store. Deshawn was free now, and she set her dead phone on the counter and asked what it would cost to just replace the battery. He turned it over, looked at the swelling along the back seam, and winced. Fifty-five dollars, and he could have it done in an hour. She heard herself say okay before she had fully decided, and then she stood at the counter sliding her card into the reader for the fifty-five, watching the little hourglass, and her stomach tightened because she was suddenly unsure, for no reason she could name, whether the two hundred and twelve was all still there, whether the overdraft from the book she'd ordered in August had ever actually cleared.

The screen read APPROVED. She let out a breath she hadn't noticed holding.

"The savings account," she said, while Deshawn pried the back off her phone, "the one that compounds monthly. Can you switch somebody into that from here?"

"Wrong building," he said, not looking up. "But it's twenty feet."

"I know where it is," Vanessa said, and picked up the dead phone, and the pen she still hadn't returned, and walked out toward the double doors with the deposit slip folded in her fist.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper 'The Strength of Weak Ties' found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.
story:
The house smelled like paint and nothing else, and Emile stood in the middle of the living room holding a phone with no signal bars, listening to it ring anyway. His mother had driven to the old town that morning to collect the last box from the old house, which meant he had six hours alone in a building where his footsteps sounded like someone else's. On the third ring, Danny picked up.

"You're calling from the future," Danny said. "How's the future?"

"Empty. There's a fridge with one water bottle in it and a floor I could sleep on." Emile sat down on the floor to prove it, cross-legged, the phone on speaker between his knees. Danny was telling him about Priya's party, the one Emile had known he would miss the moment the moving truck door rolled down, and Emile found he was listening less to the words than to the background noise of a kitchen he had eaten in maybe two hundred times. When the call dropped he sat there a while, and when he tried to introspect, to look squarely at what he was feeling, the honest answer was smaller than he expected. Not grief. Something more like vertigo, the feeling of a step that isn't there.

He went out through the garage because the front door still had no screen, and that was how he met the neighbor. She was crouched at the end of her driveway, pulling tape off a cardboard box marked BOOKS, and she looked up and said, "You're the new ones. Nobody's lived in that house since the Hendersons, and that was two years." Her name was Ruth Okafor, and this was, technically, the second time they had met; she had waved once from her porch on moving day, and Emile had waved back, and neither of them had crossed the street.

She asked what he was doing with himself all summer before college, and he said nothing much, and she said, "That's a waste of a waste," which made no sense until she explained she owned the garden shop on Delancey and needed someone for the register and the watering, mornings, and could he start Thursday. He said yes before he had decided to. Walking back across the street he kept turning it over. In the old town it had taken him a year to get a job at the pool, and that was only because Danny's sister worked there. He had known Ruth Okafor for four days, one of them only as a wave.

That night he texted Priya: I got a job from the neighbor I've met twice. She replied with a screenshot, some article his old history teacher had apparently posted, with the line highlighted: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper "The Strength of Weak Ties" found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. "Mr. Halloran says this is you," she wrote. Emile read it twice, then looked it up himself, squinting at his phone in the bare room, sitting on an air mattress with his back against the wall.

It rearranged something. All through senior year he had believed that the friends you had were the whole architecture of your life, that leaving them was leaving everything, and here was evidence that the people at the edges, the waved-at neighbors, the classmates he never quite talked to, did things his closest friends could not. He thought about how Priya had gotten her bookstore job, through a woman her mother played tennis with, someone Priya had met maybe twice, and how nobody had remarked on it, because nobody remarked on the obvious. He wanted to call Danny and lay it all out, and he picked up the phone and then set it down, because it wasn't the kind of thing Danny would want a lecture about, and because Emile wasn't sure yet what he actually thought.

Thursday morning he watered forty flats of impatiens wrong, flooding three of them, and Ruth showed him again without raising her voice. At ten a woman came in looking for something virulent, her word, to kill the moss on her bricks, and Ruth steered her to a product and then, after the woman left, said, "People always want the harshest thing for the smallest problem." Emile wrote that down mentally, or thought he did. His discernment about plants was nonexistent; he couldn't tell a weed from a seedling, and twice he pulled things Ruth had to rescue. But by the second week he could run the register, and he knew the names of four regulars, and one of them, a man named Ted who repaired bicycles out of his garage, mentioned that his nephew's roommate at the college Emile was attending in the fall was in the physics program, the exact program Emile had chosen, and gave Emile the nephew's number without anyone asking.

He didn't call the number. He carried it around in his pocket for three days, on a receipt folded twice, and he wasn't sure why. Maybe because using it felt like admitting that Danny and Priya were replaceable, which they weren't, or maybe because the whole idea, that the edges of your life mattered as much as the center, still felt like a betrayal of the year he had just had, the best year, the year of Priya's basement and Danny's terrible car and the night they walked to the reservoir. It was possible, he thought, that both things were true at once and that no principle reconciled them. The strong ties carried you; the weak ones opened doors you didn't know were doors. He could hold both. He could also be wrong.

The morning his mother came back with the last box, she found him on the porch reading Granovetter's actual paper, which he had ordered used, and she asked what it was. "A guy in 1973," Emile said, "figured out people get jobs through people they barely know." She nodded slowly, the way she nodded at things she suspected were more than they sounded.

On Saturday Danny called again, the reception better this time, and told a long story about the party, and Emile laughed in the right places, sitting on the floor of a house that was starting to smell like food and cardboard and, faintly, like them. Afterward he took the receipt out of his pocket and unfolded it on his knee, the nephew's number creased into four pale squares, and dialed.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Haggadah is the book read aloud at a Passover Seder; it retells the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt.
story:
Antoine's grandmother had led the Seder for as long as anyone could remember, and this year, in February, she had handed him the Haggadah at the end of a long Sunday lunch and said only, "Your turn." He had carried the book home on the train like something that might bruise. It was a paperback, its spine cracked to whiteness, its pages soft with decades of thumbing, and when he opened it that night he felt the peculiar weight of a text that was not his to change but was now his to carry.

He spent two weeks preparing. He read the whole thing aloud in his room, twice, timing himself, marking where the Hebrew was transliterated for people like him who could sound out the letters but not slow down enough to mean them. He made a chart of the Seder's fifteen steps on a legal pad, and he practiced the blessings into his phone and played them back, wincing at his own flat delivery. His roommate Theo, who was not Jewish and had never denigrated anything in his life except cafeteria pasta, listened through the wall one night and came in to say it actually sounded kind of beautiful.

The gathering was at his uncle Daniel's house, twenty-three people, three tables pushed together in an L, the good chairs borrowed from the synagogue. Antoine arrived early with the brisket his father had made, and found his grandmother already seated near the head, smaller than he remembered, her hands folded on the tablecloth as though she had been waiting a long time. "You'll do fine," she said, which was not the same as saying it would be fine, and he understood the difference.

The trouble began almost immediately, and it was not the trouble he had rehearsed for. His cousin Maya, who was nine and had decided this year that she was too old to be given only the easy parts, had taken possession of the stack of extra Haggadot and was flipping through them with the concentration of a lawyer preparing a case. "I want the long one," she announced. "The one Tante reads. The part about the exodus, when they get out of Egypt."

"The whole point is that everyone gets a turn," her father said, a pugnacious note creeping in, as it did whenever Maya dug in her heels. "You can't just take the good parts."

But Maya had found something true, Antoine realized, listening to them argue over the spinach dip. The Haggadah retold the story of the Israelites leaving slavery in Egypt, but it did so in pieces, scattered through blessings and songs and questions, and whoever handed out the passages decided what the evening would feel like. Maya was not being greedy. She was asking how the story got told, and by whom, and whether a nine-year-old could hold the part where the sea split.

He made a decision that was not on his legal pad. Instead of assigning the readings the way his grandmother always had, oldest to youngest down the table, he went around the room and asked each person which passage they wanted, and then, where the requests collided, he split the long sections at the seams. Maya got the exodus narrative itself, all of it, because she asked first and asked hardest. His grandfather, who mumbled, got a short blessing. Uncle Daniel wanted nothing and was given, over his objection, the Four Questions, which he hadn't read since 1981 and delivered in a monotone that made the little kids laugh.

Somewhere in the middle of the meal, between the matzah ball soup and the main course, Antoine looked up from leading the Four Sons and saw his grandmother watching him with an expression he could not parse. Later, when everyone had moved to the living room and the Afikoman had been ransomed back from the cousins who had hidden it, she beckoned him into the kitchen. "You changed the order," she said.

"I did." He waited, ready to defend it, ready also to apologize.

"I want you to know I noticed," she said, and then, after a pause that lasted through the clatter of someone stacking dishes, "and that I didn't stop you." She took his wrist, briefly, the way she did, and went back toward the noise of the family, and Antoine stayed by the sink understanding that she had handed him the Seder the way you hand over anything that matters, which is to say without instructions, and that next year he would do some of it differently and not know until afterward which parts those were.

He was still standing there when Maya appeared in the doorway with her coat half on. "Next year," she said, "can we do the plagues outside? With the water?"

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
Aaron had read the message eleven times before he answered it. Maya said she liked old diners and bad coffee, so he suggested the Starlight on Route 9, which had both, and she sent back a single thumbs-up that he spent forty minutes interpreting.

He got to the diner nine minutes early, which he knew was a mistake as soon as he sat down. Nine minutes gave him time to think. He rearranged the sugar packets, put them back, and took out his phone, not to text anyone but to hold something. His father passed through the kitchen doorway behind the counter, saw him, and raised an eyebrow. Aaron's family had owned the Starlight for two generations, a lineage his father mentioned whenever anyone asked where Aaron worked, and tonight Aaron had not told Maya any of it. He had said he knew the place. That was technically true and also a kind of lie, and he sat with that while the booth vinyl squeaked under him.

She came in at six exactly, jeans and a college sweatshirt even though she was a senior like him, and she said, "You beat me here," and he said, "Only just," which was a lie too, and smaller.

They ordered. She asked about his summer and he told her about the community college physics course he'd taken, the one real ambitious thing he'd done, and he could hear himself making it sound bigger than it was. He talked about the professor's demonstrations, a thing with a pendulum, and she listened with her chin on her hand. When he ran out of demonstrations he asked about her, and she said she'd been rejected from her first-choice school in March and had decided not to be bitter about it, and the way she said it made him think she was still deciding.

The coffee arrived. Aaron reached for his cup at the same moment Maya shifted her elbow, and the cup went over, a brown sheet across the table, coffee running into the saucer and the napkin dispenser and the edge of her sweatshirt's sleeve.

"I'm so sorry," he said. He was up with paper napkins before she'd moved. "That's, wow, that's exactly how I wanted this to go."

"It's fine," she said, dabging at her sleeve. "It's old."

"I've ruined your shirt. I've ruined the table. My dad owns this place and now I've ruined the table."

She laughed then, a short surprised sound, and he realized he'd told her the thing he'd decided not to tell her, and that it had landed better than anything he'd rehearsed. He kept wiping. His father drifted over with a rag, said nothing, gave Maya a nod, and drifted away. Aaron sat back down with a wet handful of napkins and no cup.

"Here's a thing," Maya said. "In 1966, this psychologist, Elliot Aronson, ran an experiment. There's a quiz contestant who comes off as really competent, and then the contestant spills a cup of coffee. Afterward people rated the contestant more likable. It's called the pratfall effect." She shrugged. "Screwing up in front of someone can actually help. My sister studies psych."

"So you're saying I did that on purpose."

"I'm saying you have terrible aim."

He wanted to say that he didn't believe her, that people malign psychology findings to make themselves feel better about small disasters, that a study from 1966 with one contestant couldn't stand for every spilled cup in every diner. But he also wanted to believe her, because the evening had changed when the coffee went over. Before it he had been performing a version of himself, competent Aaron, physics-course Aaron, and the performance was rigid and he could feel it straining. After it he was just a guy with wet napkins, and that guy was easier to be, more ductile, bending where the other one would have snapped.

"Maybe," he said. "Or maybe it only works for the competent person. Maybe if I hadn't spent ten minutes talking about that physics course, you'd just think I'm clumsy and boring."

"You did spend ten minutes on the physics course."

"I know."

"It was kind of sweet," she said. "The pendulum thing."

His father brought two fresh cups without being asked and set them down far from Aaron's elbow, on Maya's side. He gave Aaron a look that Aaron could not read at all, or could read in two opposite ways. Aaron put his hands in his lap and let Maya take hers first.

They stayed until the pie case went dark at eight. Outside, under the buzzing sign, she said, "This was better than the coffee deserved," and he couldn't tell if that meant there would be another one, and he decided, while unlocking his bike, that not knowing was tolerable. She was still standing there when he looked back.

"Text me when you're home," she said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The arena smelled like burnt pretzels and cold rubber, and Audrey had claimed the end of the row so she could see the whole ice instead of just the corner where her little brother kept pointing. The championship game had forty seconds left in the third period and her uncle's college team was up by one, and everyone around her, her mother, her uncle Dale, her cousin Priya, and Priya's friend Marcus, was leaning forward as though proximity could help.

Marcus was the loudest. He had never set foot on ice in his life; he'd come because Priya came, and he'd spent the first period asking what icing meant and the second period shouting coaching advice he clearly invented. Now he gripped the rail in front of them, knuckles pale, and when the goalie smothered a rebound with eleven seconds left, Marcus screamed, "Come on, we got this, we got this."

Audrey heard it and felt something snag in her mind, the way a sleeve catches on a nail. We. He said we. She had read something about that, late one night in October, in her psychology textbook's chapter on social identity, and she hadn't thought about it since. The clock hit zero, the crowd surged, and Marcus threw his arms around Priya and shouted, "We won! We won!" while her uncle wept openly into his scarf.

Outside, in the slush of the parking lot, everyone rehashed the game. Marcus narrated the final penalty kill as though he'd been on the bench for it, and Audrey watched him, feeling uncharitable and curious at once. "You said 'we' the whole third period," she said, not quite a question. "You've never even skated."

"It's the team," Marcus said. "It's, like, our school kind of. My cousin went there." He said it cheerfully, unembarrassed, and Priya laughed, and Audrey's mother told her not to interrogate guests. But it wasn't interrogation. She genuinely wanted to know why the word had bothered her when it clearly bothered her, when the truth was she'd said "we" too, once, in the second period, and then caught herself and switched to "they scored," and she couldn't say why the switch had felt like honesty rather than distance.

That night she found her textbook in the stack by her bed, its spine cracked from the fall semester, and turned back to the pages she'd half-read at midnight. There it was, in a paragraph about group identity: a 1976 study by a researcher named Robert Cialdini. After the university football team won, students wore more of the school's clothing. And when students described the games, they said "we" more when talking about wins than about losses. She read it twice. The words on the page had a provenance she could trace, a citation, a year, a method, and they described exactly what she'd watched happen in section twelve, row F, with the pretzel smell and the screaming.

She sat with it for a while, her desk lamp making a small bright territory in the dark room. Part of her wanted to text Marcus immediately, to hold the finding up like evidence at a trial, because there was a pleasure in catching someone in something. But that pleasure felt thin, almost evanescent, there and gone as soon as she noticed it. The study wasn't about Marcus being a fraud. Marcus knew he hadn't played. Everyone knew. He said "we" anyway, openly, joyfully, and nobody was deceived, least of all himself. The study was about something larger and stranger, about how a win could seep into people and make them claim a connection that a loss would leave them quietly dropping, like a hand letting go of a rail.

The next morning her uncle was still floating. He wore the team hoodie to breakfast, which he had not worn to the game, which Audrey noticed and did not say was significant, because she was watching herself now too. Over pancakes he asked what she'd thought of the ending, and she said, carefully, "Did you notice people say 'we won' but they say 'they lost'?" Her uncle frowned, half annoyed, half amused. "We had a bad period in the second," he said. "Anybody could see that." Then he went back to his coffee, and Audrey held her fork very still, because he had just done it, right there, the switch, without hearing it at all. She had done it too, last night, and the knowing didn't make her immune; that was the part she couldn't resolve.

She had two ideas in her that didn't fit together neatly, and she was honest enough with herself to admit it. One idea said the "we" was a kind of theft, secondhand glory, borrowing an achievement whose provenance was other people's years of 5 a.m. practices and stitched eyebrows and taped wrists. The other idea said that belonging was the whole point of sitting in a cold arena with your family, that the "we" was less a claim than an offering, a way of saying I'm attached to this, I'm part of the joy. The study suggested people did it without deciding to, more after wins than losses, which made it less a lie than a tide. But a tide was still not the same as a choice, and Audrey couldn't decide whether she wanted it to be.

By Monday the arena was empty again, the rink back to its public skating schedule, and Audrey went after school because Priya wanted to practice and Audrey owned skates and a vague competence. The ice was scarred and resurfaced, scarred again, its perfection from Saturday already gone, as evasive as Saturday itself. Marcus came too, wobbled along the boards, and fell twice, laughing, his palms red from the cold. When he got up the second time he said, "Okay, when I do this in college, we're going all the way." Audrey glided backward a few feet, considering him, considering her own mouth, which had almost said we.

"You could say 'I'll go all the way,'" she said. "It's your skating."

Marcus considered this with more seriousness than she expected, breath steaming, hair stuck to his forehead. "But it's better with a we," he said. Then he pushed off from the boards, arms out like a scarecrow, and Priya caught his sleeve and pulled him along, and Audrey followed, all three of them slow and unsteady and picking up speed toward the far circle.
